@@ -0,0 +1,30 @@
+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Fetch the anchor-gate corpus: ten public arXiv papers spanning the layouts that
+# actually break PDF anchoring — single and two column, dense display maths, wide
+# benchmark tables, rotated figure axis labels, and heavy use of ligatures and
+# combining diacritics.
+set -euo pipefail
+cd "$(dirname "$0")/corpus/pdf"
+
+PAPERS=(
+  1706.03762  # Attention Is All You Need — single column, wide tables
+  1810.04805  # BERT — two column, figure with rotated labels
+  1512.03385  # ResNet — two column, dense benchmark tables
+  1412.6980   # Adam — display maths throughout, stacked fractions
+  2010.11929  # ViT — rotated axis labels, many plots
+  1409.1556   # VGG — tight leading, long reference list
+  1502.03167  # Batch Normalization — inline maths in prose
+  1810.00826  # How Powerful are GNNs — theorem environments
+  2203.02155  # InstructGPT — long appendices, verbatim transcripts
+  1607.06450  # Layer Normalization — matrix displays, PUA delimiter glyphs
+)
+
+for id in "${PAPERS[@]}"; do
+  if [ -f "$id.pdf" ]; then
+    echo "have  $id.pdf"
+  else
+    echo "fetch $id.pdf"
+    curl -sSL -A "keystone-dev/0.1 (anchor test corpus)" -o "$id.pdf" "https://arxiv.org/pdf/$id"
+  fi
+done
+echo "corpus ready: $(ls -1 *.pdf | wc -l | tr -d ' ') papers"

+"""Checks over what a results table asserts internally.
+
+These need no semantic understanding of the paper and no model. They exploit the fact
+that a table makes claims beyond its numbers — that a bolded cell is the best in its
+column, that a row labelled "Average" is the average of the rows above it — and those
+claims are arithmetic, so they can simply be checked.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import re
+from collections.abc import Iterator
+from decimal import Decimal
+
+from keystone.audit.registry import check
+from keystone.graph.models import (
+    Confidence,
+    Evidence,
+    Finding,
+    Paper,
+    Severity,
+    Table,
+    TableCell,
+)
+
+# A group needs enough values for "best" to mean anything. With two, every value is
+# either the maximum or the minimum and the check can never fire.
+_MIN_GROUP_VALUES = 3
+
+# Captions that state outright what emphasis means. Direct evidence beats inference,
+# and papers say this far more often than one would expect.
+_BOLD_MEANS_BEST = re.compile(
+    r"(?:bold|boldface|underlin)\w*[^.]{0,80}?"
+    r"(?:best|highest|lowest|top|strongest|winning)"
+    r"|(?:best|highest|lowest|top|strongest|winning)[^.]{0,80}?"
+    r"(?:bold|boldface|underlin)\w*",
+    re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL,
+)
+
+# Share of emphasis the winning interpretation may leave unexplained before the
+# interpretation itself is treated as wrong. One violation is always allowed, since a
+# single slip among otherwise consistent markers is the case the check exists for.
+_MAX_UNEXPLAINED = 0.25
+
+# Markers the winning interpretation must positively explain. Without this, a table
+# with two consistent markers and one violation would report on the strength of very
+# little evidence about what emphasis means here.
+_MIN_EXPLAINED = 2
+
+# Matched against the *whole* label, never as a substring. Substring matching reads
+# "summarization" as a sum row, "avg pool" as an average row, and "small" as an all
+# row — which is how a check that cannot be wrong ends up confidently wrong.
+_AGGREGATE_LABEL = re.compile(
+    r"^(?:(?:macro|micro|weighted|grand|column|row)[\s-]*)?"
+    r"(?P<kind>total|sum|overall|average|avg|mean)\.?$",
+    re.IGNORECASE,
+)
+_SUM_KINDS = {"total", "sum", "overall"}
+
+
+@check(
+    "table.emphasis_not_best",
+    "Highlighted value is not the best among the values it is compared against",
+    description=(
+        "A bolded or underlined cell that is neither the largest nor the smallest "
+        "value in its comparison group cannot be the best under any convention."
+    ),
+)
+def emphasis_not_best(paper: Paper) -> Iterator[Finding]:
+    """Bolding a result asserts it is the best; that assertion is checkable.
+
+    Two things are deliberately *not* assumed.
+
+    **Direction.** Whether a column is an accuracy (higher is better) or an error rate
+    (lower is better) never has to be known: under either reading the best value is an
+    extreme of its group. A highlighted value strictly between the largest and smallest
+    is wrong either way, so the check never produces a finding that depends on having
+    guessed the metric's polarity.
+
+    **Orientation.** Tables come both ways. Where methods are rows and metrics are
+    columns, bold marks the best down a column; where model variants are columns, it
+    marks the best across a row. Assuming one produced 31 confident findings on a
+    single correct table. So both are tested, the better-fitting one is used, and if
+    neither explains most of the emphasis then bold does not mean "best" in this table
+    at all — it may mark the authors' own method, or a group heading — and the check
+    says nothing.
+    """
+    yield from _emphasis_findings(paper)
+
+
+def _emphasis_findings(paper: Paper) -> Iterator[Finding]:

+# Keystone
+
+**Which claim is holding the paper up, and does it hold?**
+
+Not "chat with a PDF". Keystone parses a paper's *argument* — claims, evidence,
+assumptions, citations — runs deterministic verification over it, and makes every
+answer either locked to pixel coordinates or visibly marked as unsupported. The name
+is the thesis: a keystone is the one stone that holds an arch together, and the
+product's job is to find which claim that is and test whether it bears the load.
+
+Full design and roadmap: `~/.claude/plans/rosy-humming-avalanche.md`.
+
+## Landscape
+
+Two things are true and worth stating plainly.
+
+The mainstream tools — SciSpace, ChatPDF, Elicit, Paperguide, NotebookLM — are all the
+same pipeline: chunk, embed, retrieve, answer, cite a page number. They compete on
+corpus size and polish, not capability.
+
+But Keystone is *not* the first tool to pin paper criticism to the page.
+[Loupe](https://github.com/AIScientists-Dev/loupe) (Apache 2.0) reviews scientific
+papers in a cheap triage pass followed by an opt-in deep dive, and pins every finding
+to a bounding box verified by a vision model. Someone converging independently on
+pixel-pinned findings is evidence the direction is right. Where Keystone differs:
+
+| | Loupe | Keystone |
+|---|---|---|
+| Verdicts | LLM judgement | **Deterministic code** — statcheck/GRIM recompute, arithmetic re-derivation, abstract↔table tracing |
+| Localization | MinerU → markdown, vision pass confirms the box | **Word geometry**, measured: 99.94% verified, 0/359 fabrications anchored |
+| Source of truth | OCR'd markdown | **arXiv LaTeX source** — exact equations, table numbers, `\cite` keys |
+| Citations | flags "citation required" | **fetches the cited paper** and checks entailment |
+| Finding structure | flat severity-ranked list | **claim DAG with load-bearing ranking** |
+| Emphasis | proof and reasoning defects | **empirical defects** — baseline fairness, leakage, variance, SOTA scope |
+
+Loupe's issue taxonomy (logic, quantifier scope, missing step) is oriented at proofs.
+Keystone's is oriented at experiments, which is where ML/CS papers actually go wrong.
+
+## Status
+
+**Phase 0 (substrate) — anchor gate passed.** The trust primitive is built and
+measured. Nothing here calls an LLM yet; it is all deterministic geometry and text.
+
+| Metric | Result | Gate |
+|---|---|---|
+| Tight anchors surviving independent geometric round-trip | **99.94%** (1755/1756) | ≥ 99% |
+| Approximate anchors meeting their weaker contract | **100%** (89/89) | — |
+| Real spans wrongly rejected | **0** of 1845 | 0 |
+| Anchors landing on the wrong words | **0** of 1845 | 0 |
+| Fabricated quotes wrongly anchored | **0** of 359 | 0 |
+| arXiv LaTeX source sentences anchored into the PDF | **93.5%** (2666/2852) | ≥ 90% |
+
+Measured over ten arXiv papers spanning the layouts that actually break anchoring:
+one and two column, dense display maths, wide benchmark tables, rotated axis labels,
+ligatures and combining diacritics.
+
+**Phase 1 (audit engine) — first deterministic checks landed.** Two checks run over
+tables built from arXiv LaTeX source, with no model in the loop and no network:
+
+| Metric | Result |
+|---|---|
+| Findings on nine unmodified, heavily reviewed papers | **0** |
+| Recall on deliberately planted defects | **11%** (1/9) |
+| Collateral findings caused by one planted defect | **0** |
+
+The recall number is the honest one and the operating point is deliberate. A sweep of
+the premise parameters showed the only configurations reaching 33% recall also produced
+three or four false positives across the same nine papers. For a tool whose entire
+claim is that its findings can be checked rather than trusted, that is the wrong trade.
+
+**Not yet built:** the persistence layer (Postgres + pgvector, docker-compose), claim
+and prose extraction, citation faithfulness, and the reader UI. Persistence is
+deliberately deferred until there is extracted structure to store.
+
+## Why the anchor layer got this much attention
+
+Every downstream claim depends on it. A finding that says "the abstract reports 94.2%
+but Table 3 says 93.8%" is worthless unless the reader can click it and land on both
+numbers. Getting there took several rounds of measurement, and the interesting part
+was that the first three failures were in the *test*, not the code:
+
+- Round-trip started at **67.6%**. Cause: a tall `(` from a display formula
+  legitimately clips into a body line, breaking exact string containment.
+- Union bounding boxes let one tall glyph (`→∞`) stretch a line's highlight over the
+  whole of the *next* line. Real defect; fixed with median line boxes.
+- Content-stream word order and clipped-text order genuinely differ across columns
+  and table rows, so any whole-span ordering assertion is invalid. Now checked per
+  rectangle, where order is unambiguous — a stricter test, not a looser one.
+- **Fuzzy matching accepted 5.9% of fabricated quotes** while matching zero of 1846
+  real spans. `partial_ratio` scores the best window, so a single substituted word

+Expanding from 9 papers to 35 was the first real test the check suite had, and it

+  of caption and drops those tables, which removed 56 of the 69.

+  and task-agnostic metrics"); one bolds correlations in a column whose values straddle
+  zero. In every case the premise is a convention the check cannot establish.

+the largest nor smallest of its group cannot be best under either polarity. Soundness
+was never the problem; the premise was, and on nine hand-picked papers it happened to
+hold. A check whose findings cannot be vouched for must not ship, because the suite's
+precision is the product's entire claim.

+arithmetic still catches planted defects, and one asserts that it *does* fire on
+unmodified papers. If a future premise fix makes the second test fail, the check has
+earned its place back and the test should be deleted with it.

+library shares that directory — so `keystone expand` silently quadrupled what every
+gate measured and a regression threshold changed meaning without anyone touching a

+The stance rules were the closed loop that got measured. The assumption layer was in

+| | sentences | flagged | of those, right |

+| BioScope full papers | 2,566 | 19 (0.7%) | **68.4%** [46–85%] |

+would be dishonest.** BioScope marks every sentence whose claim is qualified — "these
+results may indicate a role for X" is hedging and is annotated. Keystone looks for the
+narrower case of a paper announcing something it is *taking as given* and moving past.
+Hedged reporting of a finding is not that. Recall against BioScope is 2.5% and 1.5%,
+and that is the design showing up in the measurement rather than a defect.
+

+condition, and the two mean opposite things: *"retained the virus in the latent state
+for as long as 45 days"* is a duration, and reading it as a precondition invents an
+assumption the paper never made. Guarded, and abstracts precision went 83.8% → 86.1%.

+requiring a comparative cue to prove the citing paper was a party to the comparison,
+and BioScope has a clean case for the same idea on preconditions: *"Productive
+infection of T cells with HIV-1 typically requires that the T cells be stimulated"* is
+a fact about immunology with no "we" anywhere in it. Applying the check dropped **13 of
+the library's 23 conditional assumptions to remove that one false positive**, because a
+paper states its preconditions *about its subject matter*, not about itself — Batch
+Normalization's is *"the distributions of values of any x has the expected value of 0
+and the variance of 1, as long as the elements of each mini-batch are sampled from the
+same distribution"*, and AI safety via debate's is *"Debate only works if this revealed
+context cannot be a lie"*. Both mention nobody. The check is not in the code, and

Score the assumption cues against BioScope too

The stance rules were the closed loop that got measured; the assumption
layer was in the same one. BioScope marks every speculation cue in 2,566
sentences of biomedical full papers and 11,858 abstracts, so it can be
pointed at the question.

  full papers  flagged 19 of 2,566 (0.7%), 68.4% right [46-85%]

Not comparable to CoNLL-2010's ~85% F1 and the output says so. BioScope

The disagreements were the point, and two came back into the code:

- Fixed: "as long as" takes a quantity as readily as a condition, and the
  two mean opposite things. "retained the virus in the latent state for as
  long as 45 days" is a duration. Abstracts precision 83.8% -> 86.1%.
- Not fixed, deliberately: requiring a conditional cue to sit near a
  first-person subject -- the check that works so well for comparative cues
  -- drops 13 of the library's 23 conditional assumptions to remove one
  false positive. A paper states its preconditions about its subject matter,
  not about itself; Batch Normalization's central assumption mentions
  nobody. tests/test_hedging.py holds two such sentences so the idea does
  not get tried again.

Ten of the twelve remaining disagreements are assumptions BioScope simply
does not annotate, so both figures are a floor rather than an estimate.
Nothing from this goes on the site: the tasks differ, and the assumption
panel claiming an accuracy it did not measure is the thing this whole

Give every reading its own link, and fix the download pacing

Two things, both found by measuring rather than guessing.

**Link to one reading.** The claim this project makes is that every line is
checkable, which is hollow if checking one means telling somebody to open a
paper and scroll. Each citation and assumption now has a stable id -- from
the citation key or a hash of the sentence, never a list position, so a link
shared today still works after the cues are retuned. Following one opens the
section the row lives in, lands on it, and marks it for a few seconds.

Three things had to be got right and none was obvious:

- A closed section does not render its children, so the browser's own
  fragment jump lands on nothing. Sections now recognise their own rows.
- Scrolling once is not enough: the sections above expand for a few hundred
  milliseconds afterwards and carry the row back off screen. It now scrolls
  until the row holds still.
- `behavior: "smooth"` made it worse, not better. Each corrective scroll
  interrupted the one before it, so the row took seven seconds to arrive
  instead of two tenths of one. Measured both ways.
- The mark is set on an attribute rather than by `:target`, which does not
  reliably match an element that was absent when the fragment was parsed.

**Pacing.** Expansions were landing 8 to 12 papers out of 25 to 30, the rest
refused with HTTP 406. I had been calling that an arXiv limit. It was mine:
re-fetching six of the refused ids 20 seconds apart succeeded six times out
of six. POLITE_DELAY 6s -> 20s, and it is not even a trade -- a refusal cost
the six seconds plus a retry ladder climbing to 93, so impatience was slower
per paper as well as losing two thirds of them. First run at the new rate:
13 fetched, 1 skipped.

Stop sentences spanning the breaks the page puts in

An audit found lineage anchoring had slipped to 89% as the library grew, and
that it was not explained by source/PDF alignment -- papers below 90%
alignment anchored at 86%, those above at 89%. So the failures were per
sentence, and the worst paper sat at 56% with 95% alignment.

The cause: a sentence was allowed to span places the page breaks but the
source does not. Four kinds, each found by fixing the one before it:

- Run-in headings. "\noindent\textbf{LSTM layer:}" reads as prose and sets
  as a heading, so a sentence across one glued the sentence before to the
  sentence after and produced a quote the paper does not contain. Four of
  those were published.
- Environment boundaries. With \end{itemize} left in, the period before it
  is followed by a backslash rather than a capital, so the splitter never
  broke at all.
- The abbreviation rule undoing the fix. "\item ...Bahdanau et al. \item
  Parsing." ends its first item mid-abbreviation, which read as
  mid-sentence and glued the items back together. A hard boundary is now
  hard.
- A colon lead-in is NOT one of these. "We use the following text corpora:
  \item BookCorpus [cite]" is one statement, and breaking it cost RoBERTa
  the edge saying it adopts BookCorpus. Kept together -- but only the
  item's first sentence, since the rest of the item is its own remark. The
  test uses RoBERTa's real source, optional argument and spacing command
  included, because both leaked into the lead-in and stopped it ending in a
  colon.

  lineage anchored  89% -> 92%
  assumptions       86% -> 89%
  fabricated quotes    4 -> 0
  worst paper       56% -> 89%
  walkable edges   120 -> 119

The lost edge is a false positive: it was cued on "following" from "we
compared the following", which is a list lead-in and not an adoption.

Show how any two papers in the library relate

Borrowed from Inciteful's literature connector, which finds a citation path
between two papers. There the edges are untyped, so a path only proves the
two are connected. Here every edge carries a stance read out of the citing
sentence, so the same path is a chain of claims and the chain is the answer:

  LLaMA       adopts     Attention Is All You Need   placed by "based on"
  Transformer adopts     Deep Residual Learning      placed by "We employ"
  ResNet      builds on  Very Deep Convolutional     placed by "inspired by"

That is LLaMA's architecture traced back to VGG, and nothing in the library
said so before -- each hop was visible on its own paper's page and the chain
was not visible anywhere.

Details that matter:

- Citation is directional, reading is not. A reader asking how two papers
  relate does not care which cites which, so the search walks both ways --
  but records which way each edge points, because "A adopts B" and "B is
  adopted by A" are different sentences.
- Four hops maximum. Further than that a path through 74 papers connects
  almost anything to anything and stops explaining, so none is offered
  rather than a long one being dressed up as an explanation.
- Shortest rather than strongest: a long chain of weak links is not a better
  answer than no chain, it is a worse one, because it looks like an answer.
- The destination picker offers only papers actually reachable, and says how
  many. Offering an unreachable one is offering a question with no answer.
- Quotes are clamped to three lines rather than cut. BERT's runs to three
  hundred words and four stacked is a wall; the whole text stays in the
  document so it still copies whole.

Verified against the real graph: BERT->ResNet in two hops, LLaMA->VGG in
three, 62 of 74 reachable from BERT, a paper to itself returns nothing.

Icons for the paper actions, and a search that reads the sentences

**Icons.** Drawn rather than taken from a set: an icon library brings its own
conventions -- 2px rounded strokes on a 24px grid -- and next to type this
thin they read as pasted in from elsewhere. These are 1.25px on 16px, about
the weight of the text beside them, and they inherit currentColor so they
hover with it. Each keeps a label, because an icon alone is a guess about
what the reader already knows. The bar is 34px instead of 40.

**Search, on every page, over the sentences.** Searching a paper collection
by title is close to useless -- a reader who knows the title knows where to
go. The question worth answering is "does anything here argue with layer
normalisation", and the answer is in the sentences, which is the one thing
this project has and a title index does not. 899 lines: every stanced
citation and every assumption. A hit lands on that line, using the row ids
the deep links already use.

Two things that took measuring:

- Ranking. "layer normalization" first returned every line of the *Layer
  Normalization* paper, because its title matched and so every line of it
  did -- burying the Transformer sentence that actually says the words. The
  sentence ranks first now, then the cue or the cited work, and a paper's
  title last: a title match is the weakest hit there is, being true of every
  line that paper has.
- One sentence, one result. "We employ a residual connection [He et al.
  2016]... followed by layer normalization [Ba et al. 2016]" is genuinely
  two readings and was showing twice, which reads as a bug.

**A guide, and the reason it cannot lie.** Ask a question and it points at
the lines that bear on it. The model never writes a quotation: retrieval
picks candidates by keyword, the model replies with *numbers* plus its own
sentence about why each matters, and the server resolves those numbers back
to the stored rows. An invented number is dropped; an invented quote is
impossible, because the text on screen never passes through the model. The
panel says which line is the model's and which are the papers'.

Without a key the guide says so and search still works.

The search index shares a hash with the reader, computed in Python when the
index is written and in TypeScript when the row is rendered. Nothing fails
loudly if they drift -- results just scroll to nothing -- so
tests/test_search_index.py pins known values from both.

Make the papers selectable, which is what highlighting needs

Until now a page was pixels and nothing else: you could not select a
sentence, copy a quotation, or mark anything. pdf.js draws to canvas, so
there was no text to reach. This adds its text layer -- invisible,
absolutely positioned spans sitting exactly over the drawn glyphs -- so the
browser's own selection lands on real text.

Useful on its own: you can now take a quotation out of a paper. It is also
the foundation notes and highlights need, and it shares the rect coordinate
space the extracted readings already use, so a highlight will be able to
know which reading it overlaps without anything having to infer it.

The sizing rules are pdf.js's own and have to be. The renderer and the
stylesheet split the work: pdf.js writes --font-height, --scale-x and
--rotate onto each span, and the CSS turns those into font-size and
transform. My hand-written CSS omitted them, so every span fell back to the
page's inherited 16px serif. That measured as spans overflowing 513px past
the right edge of a 348px page while vertical placement was perfect -- and
the asymmetry is the tell, because positions come from the renderer and
sizes from the stylesheet. With their rules: zero overflow on all 59 spans.

The layer renders at layout scale, not RENDER_SCALE. The canvas is
rasterised at 1.6x for sharpness; getting this wrong puts selection a fifth
of a page from the words. Re-laid out on zoom, keyed on element and width so
scrolling past a page does not rebuild it. Outside the inverting filter,
which belongs to the picture of the page and not to transparent text.

Verified: selecting a range returns the abstract verbatim, the brass
selection lands on the drawn glyphs, and zoom tracks (scale factor
0.438 -> 0.569 as the page goes 268px -> 348px).

Read the free store before the metered one

Two Upstash databases are configured and both work. UPSTASH_* is the one
provisioned directly at upstash.com, which is where the free tier lives --
Vercel's marketplace flow offers only Pay-As-You-Go and the Fixed plans,
with no free option in the list. KV_* is that marketplace resource.

The old order put KV_* first, so the metered store would have won and the
free one would never have been read. That is the kind of mistake that
surfaces as a bill rather than as a bug.

Verified both by writing and reading a key against each endpoint before
changing anything, so this is a choice between two working stores rather
than a guess about which is live. The marketplace resource should be
disconnected now, since two stores means data lands in whichever one
resolves first.

+"""
+Analyse an arXiv paper that is not in the library, on demand.
+
+The library is seventy-four papers chosen by hand, and that is the honest limit of a
+demonstration: a reader's own paper is never in it. This route removes that limit.
+Given an arXiv id it downloads the paper's LaTeX source and its PDF, runs the same
+parser the library was built with, and returns the same dossier shape the reader
+already knows how to draw — cue phrases, stances, assumptions, and pixel anchors.
+
+Nothing is approximated to make this fit in a request. It is the same code path,
+measured at about a second and a half end to end for a paper the size of T5, which is
+why it can be a request at all rather than a queue.
+
+Two things are deliberately not done here. Citations are not resolved against the
+library's own papers, so an on-demand paper does not join the lineage graph — that
+needs every paper's full title in hand and is a build-time job. And nothing is written
+to the library: the result is cached and served, not published.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import base64
+import json
+import os
+import re
+import sys
+import time
+import traceback
+import urllib.error
+import urllib.request
+import zlib
+from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler
+from pathlib import Path
+from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlparse
+
+#: arXiv's modern form, and its older one. Anything else is refused before a single
+#: request leaves this function — an id is about to become a URL and a cache key.
+NEW_STYLE = re.compile(r"^\d{4}\.\d{4,5}(v\d+)?$")
+OLD_STYLE = re.compile(r"^[a-z-]+(\.[A-Z]{2})?/\d{7}(v\d+)?$")
+
+#: A cached dossier is worth keeping for a long time: the paper does not change, and
+#: the expensive part is arXiv's patience rather than ours. Thirty days.
+CACHE_TTL = 60 * 60 * 24 * 30
+
+#: A source tarball larger than this is somebody's 200MB collection of figures, and
+#: unpacking it inside a function with a 60-second budget ends one way.
+MAX_SOURCE = 40 * 1024 * 1024
+MAX_PDF = 40 * 1024 * 1024
+
+AGENT = "keystone/0.1 (+https://github.com/Srikarmk/Keystone)"
+
+
+def valid(arxiv_id: str) -> bool:
+    return bool(NEW_STYLE.match(arxiv_id) or OLD_STYLE.match(arxiv_id))
+
+
+def read_id(raw: str) -> str:
+    """The id out of whatever the reader pasted — a bare id, or any arXiv URL."""
+    text = (raw or "").strip()
+    if not text:
+        return ""
+    # abs/, pdf/, with or without a version, with or without the scheme.
+    found = re.search(
+        r"arxiv\.org/(?:abs|pdf|format)/([a-zA-Z0-9./-]+?)(?:v\d+)?(?:\.pdf)?/?$", text
+    )
+    if found:
+        text = found.group(1)
+    text = re.sub(r"^arxiv:", "", text, flags=re.I).strip()
+    # The version is dropped: the parser reads whatever arXiv serves as current, so
+    # keying the cache on a version it did not honour would be a lie.
+    text = re.sub(r"v\d+$", "", text)
+    return text
+
+
+# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
+# The cache. Redis over HTTP, spoken to with urllib — the same protocol and the same
+# store the reading lists use, so there is one database to reason about and no client
+# library to keep current.
+# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
+
+ENDPOINT = os.environ.get("UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL") or os.environ.get("KV_REST_API_URL")
+TOKEN = os.environ.get("UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_TOKEN") or os.environ.get("KV_REST_API_TOKEN")
+
+
+def redis(*words: object) -> object:
+    if not ENDPOINT or not TOKEN:
+        return None
+    request = urllib.request.Request(
+        ENDPOINT,
+        data=json.dumps(list(words)).encode(),
+        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}", "Content-Type": "application/json"},
+    )
+    try:
+        with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=8) as response:
+            return json.loads(response.read()).get("result")
+    except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001
+        # A cache that is down must not take the feature with it.
+        return None
+
+
+def key(arxiv_id: str) -> str:
+    return f"keystone:ingest:{arxiv_id}"
+
+
+def cached(arxiv_id: str) -> bytes | None:
+    stored = redis("GET", key(arxiv_id))
+    if not isinstance(stored, str):
+        return None
+    try:
+        return zlib.decompress(base64.b64decode(stored))
+    except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001
+        return None
+
+
+def remember(arxiv_id: str, payload: bytes) -> None:
+    # Stored compressed. A dossier is around 650KB of JSON and about 55KB deflated,
+    # which is the difference between fitting in a Redis value comfortably and
+    # arguing with a size limit on every large paper.
+    packed = base64.b64encode(zlib.compress(payload, 6)).decode()
+    redis("SET", key(arxiv_id), packed, "EX", CACHE_TTL)
+
+
+# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
+# The work itself.
+# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
+
+
+def fetch(url: str, limit: int) -> bytes:
+    request = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": AGENT})
+    with urllib.request.urlopen(request, timeout=45) as response:
+        payload = response.read(limit + 1)
+    if len(payload) > limit:
+        raise ValueError("that paper's files are larger than this will download")
+    return payload
+
+
+def build(arxiv_id: str) -> dict:
+    """Download, parse, anchor. The same call the command line makes."""
+    from keystone import dossier as dossier_module
+    from keystone.ingest.arxiv_source import SourceUnavailable
+
+    work = Path("/tmp/keystone")
+    cache = work / "cache"
+    pdfs = work / "pdf"
+    cache.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
+    pdfs.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

reading lists use, deflated - 674KB of JSON is 55KB compressed.

imported nowhere (render draws through PyMuPDF's own pixmaps) and cost 107MB
of a 192MB install, which does not matter on a laptop and does inside a

@@ -0,0 +1,83 @@
+"""A mismatch must name the cell it accuses.
+
+`reporting.headline_table_mismatch` is the strongest statement this project makes
+about a paper: that a number in the abstract is not the number the paper's own table
+carries. It is published at high severity and likely confidence, so it has to be right
+far more often than not.
+
+What separates a real one from a coincidence is the row header. With a row, the finding
+names a cell and a reader can go and look — EfficientNet's introduction says 76.3% for
+ResNet-50 where its Table 3 says 76.0%, and that is checkable in ten seconds. Without
+one, the claim is only that *some* value under a similarly-named column differs, which
+in a multi-row table is what you would expect even when the paper is entirely correct.
+
+Measured when the library went from 74 papers to 101: seven mismatches, two with a row
+and five without. Both with a row were real; all five without were a headline number
+paired against another configuration's row — Megatron-LM's 76% scaling efficiency
+against a 77% cell, MBPP's 59.6% few-shot result against a 59.0% cell for a different
+model size.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+from decimal import Decimal
+
+from keystone.audit.numbers import Number
+from keystone.audit.trace import Coverage, Trace, mismatch_findings
+from keystone.graph.models import NumericMention, SectionKind, Table, TableCell
+
+
+def _mismatch(row_header: str) -> Coverage:
+    """One headline number against one table cell, differing beyond rounding."""
+    def percent(text: str) -> Number:
+        return Number(
+            value=Decimal(text),
+            raw=f"{text}%",
+            start=0,
+            end=len(text) + 1,
+            decimals=0,
+            quantum=Decimal("1"),
+            is_percent=True,
+        )
+
+    cell = TableCell(
+        row=1,
+        column=1,
+        raw="77",
+        number=percent("77"),
+        row_header=row_header,
+        column_header="Scaling Efficiency",
+    )
+    table = Table(ordinal=6, caption="Scaling", cells=(cell,))
+    mention = NumericMention(
+        number=percent("76"),
+        sentence="We sustain 76% scaling efficiency across the application.",
+        section=SectionKind.ABSTRACT,
+    )
+    return Coverage(
+        traces=(
+            Trace(
+                mention=mention,
+                status="mismatch",
+                table=table,
+                cell=cell,
+                context_score=2,
+            ),
+        ),
+        keystone=None,
+    )
+
+
+def test_a_mismatch_with_a_named_row_is_reported() -> None:
+    findings = mismatch_findings(_mismatch("ResNet-50"))
+    assert len(findings) == 1
+    assert findings[0].arithmetic["row"] == "ResNet-50"
+
+
+def test_a_mismatch_with_no_row_is_not_reported() -> None:
+    """The five false accusations that arrived with the library's expansion."""
+    assert mismatch_findings(_mismatch("")) == []
+
+
+def test_a_whitespace_row_is_no_row() -> None:
+    assert mismatch_findings(_mismatch("   ")) == []

A mismatch must name the cell it accuses

Growing the library from 74 papers to 101 produced seven headline-vs-table
mismatches. Two named a row and were real - EfficientNet's introduction says
76.3% for ResNet-50 where its Table 3 says 76.0%, and you can go and look.
Five named no row at all, and every one of those had paired a headline number
against a different configuration's row in a multi-row table: Megatron-LM's
76% scaling efficiency against a 77% cell, MBPP's 59.6% few-shot result
against a 59.0% cell belonging to another model size.

Five false accusations against two true ones is not a rate this can publish
at, and these go out at high severity. Without a row header the claim is only
that some value under a similarly-named column differs, which in a multi-row
table is what you would expect of a correct paper. So the finding now requires
the cell to be nameable, and three tests pin it.

+{
+  "id": "1212.5701",
+  "title": "ADADELTA: An Adaptive Learning Rate Method",
+  "sections": [
+    {
+      "kind": "abstract",
+      "title": "Abstract",
+      "text": "We present a novel per-dimension learning rate method for gradient descent called ADADELTA. The method dynamically adapts over time using only first order information and has minimal computational overhead beyond vanilla stochastic gradient descent. The method requires no manual tuning of a learning rate and appears robust to noisy gradient information, different model architecture choices, various data modalities and selection of hyperparameters. We show promising results compared to other methods on the MNIST digit classification task using a single machine and on a large scale voice dataset in a distributed cluster environment."
+    },
+    {
+      "kind": "introduction",
+      "title": "Introduction",
+      "text": "The aim of many machine learning methods is to update a set of parameters in order to optimize an objective function . This often involves some iterative procedure which applies changes to the parameters, at each iteration of the algorithm. Denoting the parameters at the -th iteration as , this simple update rule becomes: x_t+1 = x_t + x_t In this paper we consider gradient descent algorithms which attempt to optimize the objective function by following the steepest descent direction given by the negative of the gradient . This general approach can be applied to update any parameters for which a derivative can be obtained: x_t = - g_t where is the gradient of the parameters at the -th iteration and is a learning rate which controls how large of a step to take in the direction of the negative gradient. Following this negative gradient for each new sample or batch of samples chosen from the dataset gives a local estimate of which direction minimizes the cost and is referred to as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) . While often simple to derive the gradients for each parameter analytically, the gradient descent algorithm requires the learning rate hyperparameter to be chosen. Setting the learning rate typically involves a tuning procedure in which the highest possible learning rate is chosen by hand. Choosing higher than this rate can cause the system to diverge in terms of the objective function, and choosing this rate too low results in slow learning. Determining a good learning rate becomes more of an art than science for many problems. +# Working on Keystone
+
+Read this first. It is the operating manual — what the project is, how to run it, and
+the specific things that have cost hours here. The architecture is in `README.md`; the
+decision history is in `RELEASE.md`.
+
+## What it is
+
+Keystone reads an arXiv paper's **LaTeX source** and reports, verbatim, two things:
+what each citation *adopts / extends / disputes / measures against* (decided by cue
+phrases, not a model), and what the paper *assumes*, filed by whether the same sentence
+offers a citation, its own evidence, or nothing. Every reading is anchored to pixel
+rectangles on the PDF, and where a sentence cannot be located nothing is drawn.
+
+The governing principle is **precision over coverage**: it is silent where a sentence
+says nothing checkable, and silence is reported as silence rather than dressed up. Any
+change that trades that away is the wrong change, however much it improves a number.
+
+- Live: <https://keystone-research.vercel.app> (old name `keystone-seven-beta` 307s to it)
+- Repo: <https://github.com/Srikarmk/Keystone> — public, so never commit a secret
+
+## Where things are
+
+```
+services/core/          Python engine (parser, anchors, cue rules). 261 tests.
+  keystone/ingest/      arXiv source, PDF, anchors, metadata
+  keystone/lineage/     stance + assumption cue rules
+  keystone/audit/       numeric tracing and the deterministic checks
+apps/web/               Next 15 App Router site. 41 JS tests.
+  app/api/ingest.py     Python serverless function: analyse any arXiv paper on demand
+  public/dossiers/      the built library — 101 papers, committed
+eval/corpus/            e-print + PDF cache, metadata.json. Gitignored, not in the repo.
+```
+
+## Commands
+
+```bash
+# Python engine
+cd services/core && uv run pytest -q              # 261 tests
+cd services/core && uv run keystone --help        # the CLI
+
+# Site
+cd apps/web && npm test                           # 41 tests (node --test)
+cd apps/web && npx tsc --noEmit -p .              # typecheck
+cd apps/web && npm run build
+
+# Deploy — see the trap below, this is NOT automatic
+cd apps/web && npx vercel --prod --yes
+```
+
+## Traps that have actually cost time here
+
+These are the expensive ones. Each was found the hard way.
+
+**Deploys are manual.** A push to `main` deploys nothing — the Vercel project has no git
+integration. Always `cd apps/web && npx vercel --prod --yes` yourself. A quiet minute
+after a push means no deploy was triggered, not a slow build.
+
+**`next build` poisons `next dev`.** They share `.next`. After a build, client components
+silently stop mounting and the error names a missing chunk. `rm -rf .next` before
+starting the dev server, every time.
+
+**Next's data cache outlives deployments.** A route that fetches a built file with
+`revalidate` or `force-cache` keeps serving the *previous build's* copy. This made the
+MCP route report 40 disputes when there were 52, through a redeploy and through a fix
+that was not the cause. Use `lib/built.ts`, which keys the URL with the commit SHA.

+configured, so nothing read the request. One reader's page, served to everybody.

+# Docker Lab 1: Containerized Model Training
+
+This lab trains a Random Forest classifier on the Iris dataset inside a Docker container. The container evaluates the model on a held-out test set and writes the trained model and its metrics to a folder that is mounted from the host, so the files remain after the container exits.
+
+## Project structure
+
+```
+.
+├── dockerfile
+├── .dockerignore
+└── src/
+    ├── main.py            # trains, evaluates and saves the model
+    └── requirements.txt   # pinned dependencies
+```
+
+## Changes from the base lab
+
+| Area | Base lab | This version |
+|---|---|---|
+| Base image | `python:3.10` | `python:3.10-slim` |
+| Image size | 2.06 GB | 543 MB |
+| Dependencies | unpinned | pinned (`scikit-learn==1.7.2`, `joblib==1.6.0`, `numpy==2.2.6`) |
+| Layer caching | code and dependencies copied together | `requirements.txt` copied and installed first, so code changes don't trigger a reinstall |
+| Evaluation | none | test accuracy plus a per-class classification report |
+| Output | model saved inside the container and lost when it exits | `iris_model.pkl` and `metrics.json` written to a mounted volume |

+

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Runs the whole lab end to end: build -> save/load round trip -> train -> predict -> export.
+#
+#   ./run_lab.sh            run everything, keep the image, volume and containers afterwards
+#   ./run_lab.sh --clean    run everything, then remove the containers, image, volume and tarball
+#
+# IMAGE and VOLUME can be overridden, e.g. IMAGE=mylab:v1 ./run_lab.sh
+
+set -euo pipefail
+
+IMAGE="${IMAGE:-lab1:latest}"
+VOLUME="${VOLUME:-lab1-output}"
+TRAIN_CONTAINER="lab1-train"
+PREDICT_CONTAINER="lab1-predict"
+TARBALL="lab1-image.tar.gz"
+CLEAN=false
+[ "${1:-}" = "--clean" ] && CLEAN=true
+
+cd "$(dirname "$0")"
+
+step() { printf '\n==> %s\n' "$*"; }
+read_accuracy() {
+    docker run --rm -v "$VOLUME:/app/output" --entrypoint cat "$IMAGE" /app/output/metrics.json \
+        | grep '"accuracy"' | tr -dc '0-9.'
+}
+
+step "Checking Docker"
+if ! command -v docker >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+    echo "docker not found. Install Docker Desktop: https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/" >&2
+    exit 1
+fi
+if ! docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+    echo "Docker is installed but the daemon isn't running. Start Docker Desktop and try again." >&2
+    exit 1
+fi
+docker version --format 'Client {{.Client.Version}}, Engine {{.Server.Version}}'
+
+step "Removing containers left from a previous run"
+docker rm -f "$TRAIN_CONTAINER" "$PREDICT_CONTAINER" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
+
+step "Building $IMAGE"
+docker build -t "$IMAGE" .
+docker image ls "$IMAGE" --format 'Image size: {{.Size}}'
+
+step "Creating named volume $VOLUME"
+docker volume create "$VOLUME" >/dev/null
+docker volume inspect "$VOLUME" --format 'Mountpoint inside the Docker VM: {{.Mountpoint}}'
+
+step "Baseline training run (temporary container, removed on exit with --rm)"
+docker run --rm -v "$VOLUME:/app/output" "$IMAGE" train | grep -E 'Test (accuracy|ROC-AUC)'
+accuracy_before=$(read_accuracy)
+
+step "Saving the image to $TARBALL"
+id_before=$(docker image inspect "$IMAGE" --format '{{.Id}}')
+docker save "$IMAGE" | gzip > "$TARBALL"
+ls -lh "$TARBALL" | awk '{print "Tarball size: " $5}'
+
+step "Removing $IMAGE locally and loading it back from $TARBALL"
+docker rmi "$IMAGE" >/dev/null
+if docker image inspect "$IMAGE" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+    echo "$IMAGE is still present after docker rmi" >&2
+    exit 1
+fi
+echo "$IMAGE removed"
+gunzip -c "$TARBALL" | docker load
+id_after=$(docker image inspect "$IMAGE" --format '{{.Id}}')
+
+step "Training with the loaded image (container $TRAIN_CONTAINER, kept after it exits)"
+docker run --name "$TRAIN_CONTAINER" -v "$VOLUME:/app/output" "$IMAGE" train
+accuracy_after=$(read_accuracy)
+
+step "Predicting (container $PREDICT_CONTAINER reads the model from the same volume)"
+docker run --name "$PREDICT_CONTAINER" -v "$VOLUME:/app/output" -v "$(pwd)/samples:/app/input:ro" "$IMAGE" \
+    predict /app/input/new_samples.csv
+
+step "Checking the save/load round trip"
+echo "Image ID before save: $id_before"
+echo "Image ID after load:  $id_after"
+echo "Accuracy before: $accuracy_before, after: $accuracy_after"
+if [ "$id_before" = "$id_after" ] && [ "$accuracy_before" = "$accuracy_after" ]; then
+    echo "Round trip OK: the loaded image is identical and reproduces the same result."
+else
+    echo "Round trip mismatch." >&2
+    exit 1
+fi
+
+step "Copying the volume contents to ./output"
+mkdir -p output
+docker cp "$PREDICT_CONTAINER:/app/output/." output/
+ls -l output
+
+if $CLEAN; then
+    step "Cleaning up"
+    docker rm "$TRAIN_CONTAINER" "$PREDICT_CONTAINER" >/dev/null
+    docker rmi "$IMAGE" >/dev/null
+    docker volume rm "$VOLUME" >/dev/null
+    rm -f "$TARBALL"
+    echo "Removed containers, $IMAGE, volume $VOLUME and $TARBALL (./output is kept)"
+else
+    step "Containers kept for inspection"
+    docker ps -a --filter "name=lab1-" --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Status}}'
+    echo "View their output with: docker logs $TRAIN_CONTAINER   (or open them in Docker Desktop)"
+fi
+
+step "Done"

+# Wine Quality Prediction Lab Documentation
+
+This documentation provides a step-by-step guide to a data science lab focused on predicting wine quality using Python. The lab covers data preprocessing, model training, model registration, and batch inference using MLflow and various machine learning libraries.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+Before starting the lab, ensure that you have the following:
+
+- Python environment set up with required libraries installed.
+- Datasets: You will need two CSV files, `winequality-white.csv` and `winequality-red.csv`, containing white and red wine data, respectively.
+
+## Step 1: Importing Data
+
+In this step, we load the white and red wine datasets using the Pandas library.
+
+```python
+import pandas as pd
+
+# Load white wine data
+white_wine = pd.read_csv("data/winequality-white.csv", sep=";")
+
+# Load red wine data
+red_wine = pd.read_csv("data/winequality-red.csv", sep=",")
+```
+
+## Step 2: Exploring Data
+
+In this step, we'll explore the wine dataset by examining the first few rows of both the white and red wine datasets.
+
+### Code:
+
+```python
+white_wine.head()
+red_wine.head()
+```
+
+## Step 3: Data Preprocessing
+
+In this step, we'll perform data preprocessing tasks to prepare the wine dataset for model training.
+
+### Adding Indicator Variable
+
+We add an indicator variable 'is_red' to both datasets to distinguish between white and red wines.
+
+### Code:
+
+```python
+red_wine['is_red'] = 1
+white_wine['is_red'] = 0
+
+data = pd.concat([red_wine, white_wine], axis=0)
+
+# Remove spaces from column names
+data.rename(columns=lambda x: x.replace(' ', '_'), inplace=True)
+```
+
+## Step 4: Data Visualization
+
+In this step, we'll visualize the distribution of the 'quality' variable in the wine dataset.
+
+### Code:
+
+```python
+import seaborn as sns
+import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
+
+sns.distplot(data.quality, kde=False);
+```
+
+
+## Step 5: Define High-Quality Wines
+
+In this step, we'll define what constitutes a "high-quality" wine based on a quality score threshold.
+
+### Code:
+
+```python
+high_quality = (data.quality >= 7).astype(int)
+data.quality = high_quality
+```
+
+### Explanation:
+We create a new binary column high_quality in the data DataFrame.
+A wine is considered "high quality" if its 'quality' score is greater than or equal to 7.
+We use (data.quality >= 7) to create a boolean mask and then convert it to integers (astype(int)) to represent high-quality wines as 1 and others as 0.
+The original 'quality' column is updated with these new values.
+Expected Output:
+The data DataFrame will have a new 'quality' column indicating whether each wine is of high quality (1) or not (0).
+
+
+
+## Step 6: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
+
+In this step, we'll perform Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) by creating box plots to identify potential predictors of wine quality.
+
+### Code:

+from pathlib import Path
+
+import pandas as pd
+from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
+
+DATA_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data"
+RANDOM_STATE = 123
+
+
+def load_wine_data():
+    # The two files use different separators
+    white = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "winequality-white.csv", sep=";")
+    red = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "winequality-red.csv", sep=",")
+
+    red["is_red"] = 1
+    white["is_red"] = 0
+    data = pd.concat([red, white], axis=0, ignore_index=True)
+    data = data.rename(columns=lambda c: c.replace(" ", "_"))
+
+    # A wine is "high quality" if it scored 7 or more
+    data["quality"] = (data["quality"] >= 7).astype(int)
+    return data
+
+
+def split(data):
+    X = data.drop(columns=["quality"])
+    y = data["quality"]
+    X_train, X_rem, y_train, y_rem = train_test_split(X, y, train_size=0.6, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
+    X_val, X_test, y_val, y_test = train_test_split(X_rem, y_rem, test_size=0.5, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
+    return X_train, X_val, X_test, y_train, y_val, y_test

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Serves a registered model version over REST with `mlflow models serve`.
+#
+#   ./serve_model.sh                 serve models:/wine_quality@champion on http://127.0.0.1:5001
+#   ./serve_model.sh challenger      serve @challenger instead
+#   PORT=5002 ./serve_model.sh       use another port
+#
+# The alias is resolved once at startup: after a promotion or rollback, restart this to serve the new version.
+
+set -euo pipefail
+
+ALIAS="${1:-champion}"
+PORT="${PORT:-5001}"
+HOST="${HOST:-127.0.0.1}"
+MODEL_NAME="${MODEL_NAME:-wine_quality}"
+export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI="${MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI:-http://127.0.0.1:8080}"
+export MLFLOW_ENABLE_ARTIFACTS_PROGRESS_BAR=false
+
+cd "$(dirname "$0")"
+
+# mlflow models serve starts uvicorn from PATH, so the virtual environment has to be active
+if ! command -v uvicorn >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+    if [ -f .venv/bin/activate ]; then
+        source .venv/bin/activate
+    else
+        echo "No .venv found. Create it and install requirements.txt first (see README)." >&2
+        exit 1
+    fi
+fi
+
+if ! curl -sf "$MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI/health" >/dev/null; then
+    echo "No MLflow tracking server at $MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI. Start it first (see README)." >&2
+    exit 1
+fi
+
+echo "Serving models:/$MODEL_NAME@$ALIAS on http://$HOST:$PORT/invocations (Ctrl+C to stop)"
+# --env-manager local reuses this environment instead of building a new one from the model's requirements
+exec mlflow models serve -m "models:/$MODEL_NAME@$ALIAS" --env-manager local -h "$HOST" -p "$PORT"

+ +# Silent Failures + +**Detecting retrieval degradation in RAG systems without relevance labels** + +![Status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-proposal-f59e0b?style=flat-square) +![Course](https://img.shields.io/badge/DS5500-Fall%202026-4f46e5?style=flat-square) +![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-3776ab?style=flat-square&logo=python&logoColor=white) +![Data](https://img.shields.io/badge/data-BEIR-10b981?style=flat-square) + +[Motivation](#motivation) · [Approach](#approach) · [Failures](#failure-families) · [Detectors](#detectors) · [Evaluation](#evaluation) · [Early results](#early-results) · [Timeline](#timeline) + +
+ +## Motivation + +A RAG system embeds the user's question, finds the most similar documents in a vector index, and passes them to an LLM along with the question. If the retrieval step gets worse, nothing errors out. The system stays up and latency looks normal, but the answers get worse, and usually nobody notices for a while. + +A few ways this happens in practice: + +- an embedding model gets upgraded, but only part of the corpus is re-embedded +- outdated documents stay in the index next to their replacements +- chunking or preprocessing settings change partway through the corpus +- users start asking about things the corpus doesn't cover + +Production systems don't have relevance labels, so you can't just track nDCG. Teams rely on label-free signals instead, like drift statistics or retrieval scores, and it isn't clear which of these actually catch real damage. That is the question this project tries to answer. + +**What we plan to release** + +1. An open-source benchmark that injects realistic retrieval failures at controlled severity +2. A detector-by-failure heatmap showing which signal catches what, and how early +3. A short, practical guide to monitoring retrieval quality + +## Approach + +We build a standard retrieval pipeline, break it in controlled ways, and check whether each detector notices. The detectors only get what a production system would have: queries, embeddings and similarity scores. The labeled relevance judgments are used for one thing only, measuring how much damage each failure actually caused. + +```mermaid +flowchart LR + A[("Corpus")] --> B["Embed
sentence-transformers"] + B --> C[("FAISS index")] + Q["Queries"] --> C + C --> D["Inject failure
F1–F5, 10%–90% severity"] + D --> E["Label-free detectors"] + D --> F["nDCG@10 drop
(uses labels)"] + E --> G{"Did the detector fire
when the damage was real?"} + F --> G +``` + +## Failure families + +Each failure is applied at increasing severity, from 10% up to 90% of the corpus or query traffic. + +| ID | Failure | How we simulate it | +|---|---|---| +| F1 | Partial embedding upgrade | Mix vectors from two same-dimension models in one index | +| F2 | Stale documents | Outdated content from HoH, plus injected distractors | +| F3 | Chunking change | Re-chunk only part of the corpus | +| F4 | Query shift | Move query traffic toward topics outside the corpus | +| F5 | Config mismatch | Drop the query prefix, turn off vector normalization, etc. | + +We also run three **harmless** changes. A good detector should stay quiet on these, so they tell us its false-alarm rate. + +## Detectors + +| Family | Detectors | +|---|---| +| Drift statistics (ML) | PSI, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, MMD, domain classifier | +| Query performance prediction (IR) | Score-based signals, canary queries | +| Other | Re-embedding check, LLM-as-judge | + +If there's time, we'll also test whether an agentic retriever that searches more than usual is itself a sign of hidden damage. + +## Evaluation + +The ground truth is the drop in **nDCG@10** from the clean baseline. Each check runs on a sampled window of queries, repeated over many trials per condition. +# How we're working on this
+
+Keeping this short so we actually follow it. If something here gets in the way, bring it up and we'll change it.
+
+## Setup
+
+```bash
+python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
+pip install -e ".[dev]"
+pre-commit install
+pytest
+```
+
+`pre-commit install` sets up nbstripout, which clears notebook outputs when you commit. Without it, two people touching the same notebook means a merge conflict every time.
+
+On a Mac, if anything that uses both faiss and torch just exits with no error, run it with `KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK=TRUE OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`.
+
+## Who's on what (for now)
+
+| Area | Person | Code |
+|---|---|---|
+| Data + baseline | Jenna | `data`, `eval/ground_truth.py` |
+| Pipeline + runner | Srikar | `pipeline.py`, `run.py`, `eval/results.py` |
+| Failure injection | Shane | `inject/` |
+| Detectors | Alekhya | `detect/` |
+
+This isn't fixed. Once injection is stable (around week 4), Shane moves over to help with detectors since that's the biggest chunk. Weeks 8 to 10 we're all on the held-out run and the guide.
+
+## How the code fits together
+
+The whole thing hangs on three interfaces in `src/silent_rag/`:
+
+- **`Injector.apply(state, severity, seed)`** returns a damaged copy of the retrieval state. Severity always means fraction affected (0.1 to 0.9). Same seed, same result.
+- **`Detector.fit(reference)` / `Detector.score(window)`** take an `Observation`, which has query embeddings, top-k ids and scores, but **no qrels**. That's on purpose. If a detector needs labels, it's not label-free and it doesn't belong in this project.
+- **`ResultRow`** is one row per condition, trial and detector. Every plot comes from this table, so if you need a new column, add it there rather than making a side CSV.
+
+Qrels only get touched in `eval/ground_truth.py`.
+
+## The held-out rule
+
+We tune only on NFCorpus. SciFact and FiQA are for the final numbers. The runner won't touch them unless you pass `--final`. Please don't work around it, even "just to check something". The moment we tune on them, the results stop meaning anything.
+
+## Branches and PRs
+
+- Don't push straight to `main`. Branch, open a PR, get one review, squash merge.
+- Name branches `<area>/<what>`, like `inject/f1-partial-upgrade` or `detect/mmd`.
+- Keep branches small and short. A few days, not a few weeks.
+- Each PR should close an issue (`Closes #12` in the description).
+- Notebooks are for exploring. Anything we'll reuse goes in `src/` and gets imported into the notebook.
+- Don't commit data, embeddings or caches. They're all in `.gitignore` and can be rebuilt. Small result summaries are fine.
+
+## Issues
+
+- One issue should be about 1 to 3 days of work. If it's bigger, split it.
+- Fill in "Done when" so we know when to close it.
+- Labels: `area/*` for which part of the code, `research` for decisions we need to make together (like window size).
+- Milestones match the timeline in the README.
+
+We'll do a quick weekly sync where we go through the board and see what's stuck.

+"""BEIR loaders from the Hugging Face Hub, pinned to the revisions the EDA used.
+
+Only queries that have qrels in the chosen split are kept, so every query the
+runner sees can be scored.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+from silent_rag.types import Dataset
+
+SOURCES = {
+    "nfcorpus": {
+        "repo": "BeIR/nfcorpus",
+        "revision": "b5026a0e96e8a7ac4f95f482a596389289d46269",
+        "qrels": "BeIR/nfcorpus-qrels",
+        "qrels_revision": "a451b3b26d3ae1358f259c1a3a4dd61fcea35a65",
+    },
+    "scifact": {
+        "repo": "BeIR/scifact",
+        "revision": "b3b5335604bf5ee3c4447671af975ea25143d4f5",
+        "qrels": "BeIR/scifact-qrels",
+        "qrels_revision": "2938d17dc3b09882fdb8c12bbbe2e2dc0e75a029",
+    },
+    "fiqa": {
+        "repo": "BeIR/fiqa",
+        "revision": "979c07a7cb5ccc6ca009792241fa1250b98055dd",
+        "qrels": "BeIR/fiqa-qrels",
+        "qrels_revision": None,
+    },
+}
+
+
+def doc_text(title: str | None, text: str | None) -> str:
+    return f"{(title or '').strip()} {(text or '').strip()}".strip()
+
+
+def load(name: str, split: str = "test") -> Dataset:
+    from datasets import load_dataset
+
+    src = SOURCES[name]
+    corpus = load_dataset(src["repo"], "corpus", split="corpus", revision=src["revision"])
+    queries = load_dataset(src["repo"], "queries", split="queries", revision=src["revision"])
+    qrels_rows = load_dataset(src["qrels"], split=split, revision=src["qrels_revision"])
+
+    qrels: dict[str, dict[str, int]] = {}
+    for row in qrels_rows:
+        qrels.setdefault(str(row["query-id"]), {})[str(row["corpus-id"])] = int(row["score"])
+
+    query_text = {str(q["_id"]): q["text"] for q in queries}
+    return Dataset(
+        name=name,
+        corpus={str(d["_id"]): doc_text(d["title"], d["text"]) for d in corpus},
+        # qrels order, so query order matches the pilot runs
+        queries={q: query_text[q] for q in qrels},
+        qrels=qrels,
+    )

+# Fantasy Racer
+
+A pseudo-3D (OutRun-style) fantasy kart racer built with Next.js + TypeScript +
+Canvas 2D. No game engine, no runtime dependencies beyond React/Next.
+
+## Commands
+
+- `npm run dev` — dev server at http://localhost:3000
+- `npm run build` — production build
+- `npm run typecheck` — `tsc --noEmit`; run after engine changes
+
+## Architecture
+
+The core rule: **game logic never imports React, and React never touches game
+state.** React/Next is only the shell that mounts the canvas.
+
+- `app/` — Next.js App Router shell. `app/components/GameCanvas.tsx` is the
+  only client component; it instantiates `Game` in a `useEffect` and calls
+  `game.stop()` on unmount.
+- `src/game/` — framework-agnostic engine, plain TypeScript:
+  - `engine.ts` — `Game` class: fixed-timestep loop (60 Hz update, rAF render),
+    player driving state (position, playerX, speed)
+  - `road.ts` — track as a list of segments; `project()` does the
+    world→camera→screen perspective math
+  - `render.ts` — all canvas drawing (background, road segments, player, HUD)
+  - `input.ts` — keyboard state (arrows + WASD)
+  - `constants.ts` — tuning values and realm color palettes; tweak feel here
+
+## Rendering model (pseudo-3D)
+
+The track is segments of `SEGMENT_LENGTH` world units. Each frame, segments
+from the camera forward (`DRAW_DISTANCE` of them) are projected with
+perspective division and drawn front-to-back, clipping against `maxY` so
+hidden geometry is skipped. Curves will be faked by accumulating per-segment
+horizontal drift (phase 2) — nothing is real 3D.
+
+`playerX` is normalized: -1..1 spans the road; beyond that is off-road (grass
+drag applies).
+
+## Conventions
+
+- Speeds/positions are in world units per second; `dt` is seconds. All tuning
+  constants derive from `MAX_SPEED`/`SEGMENT_LENGTH` in `constants.ts`.
+- Canvas is fixed 800×600 logical pixels, scaled by CSS (4:3, pixelated).
+- Colors come from the `COLORS` palette object — never hardcode hex values in
+  render code, so realm themes can swap palettes later.
+
+## Roadmap
+
+See TODO.md for phase status; PLAN.md for the full design.

+# Fantasy Racer — Plan
+
+A pseudo-3D (OutRun-style) fantasy kart racer for the web.
+Vanilla JS + Canvas 2D, ES modules, Vite for dev/build. No runtime dependencies.
+
+## Concept
+
+Race a magical vehicle down winding roads through fantasy realms —
+dodge obstacles, overtake AI racers, grab power-ups. Mario Kart spirit,
+OutRun rendering.
+
+## Rendering approach
+
+The track is a list of road segments, each with a curve value and elevation.
+Each frame, segments are projected to screen space with perspective division
+and drawn back-to-front. Curves are faked by accumulating horizontal drift
+across segments. Sprites scale with the same projection.
+
+## Module layout (target)
+
+- `src/main.js` — entry, canvas setup, fixed-timestep game loop
+- `src/road.js` — track segments, projection, road rendering
+- `src/player.js` — speed, steering, centrifugal force, off-road handling
+- `src/sprites.js` — scenery/obstacle/opponent sprite drawing
+- `src/input.js` — keyboard (touch later)
+- `src/hud.js` — speed, lap, position, timer
+- `src/game.js` — state machine: title → countdown → racing → results
+
+## Roadmap (each phase ends playable)
+
+- [ ] 1. Straight road: segment renderer, stripes, forward driving
+- [ ] 2. Curves & hills + centrifugal force
+- [ ] 3. Steering, off-road slowdown, track loop with laps
+- [ ] 4. Fantasy scenery, themed realm palettes, parallax backgrounds
+- [ ] 5. AI opponents, collisions, race positions
+- [ ] 6. Power-ups: boost runes, shields, spells
+- [ ] 7. Game shell: title, realm select, countdown, results, sound
+- [ ] 8. Later: touch controls, desktop wrap (Tauri/Electron)

Grip-limited handling, camera feel & filmic grading

Rework the driving to feel physical instead of on-rails, and grade the look.

Handling (grip-limited lateral model):
- Steering asks for lateral accel; tires cap it (grip ceiling) so a too-fast
  corner washes wide — you must brake and commit to a line.
- Weight transfer (braking loads the front), steering inertia + self-centering,
  speed-sensitive steering authority, tire scrub, and visible yaw into slip.
- Car-type grip still multiplies through; drift retained with looser grip.

Camera feel:
- FOV kicks with speed / flares on boost, banks into corners, looks ahead into
  the turn, and shakes on impacts / hard landings.

Finish:
- ACES filmic tone mapping + OutputPass for richer colour and highlight roll-off.
- Asphalt-style speed overlay: vignette + radial streaks that build with speed.
- Glowing edge-marker posts line the track (real-circuit look + speed reference).

Racing-phase smoothness: cut the shadow pass cost (~20% of frame)

Diagnosis (measured live via window.__frGame): physics/update is ~0.05ms/frame
— effectively free — so the "not smooth" is entirely render cost (~27ms/frame
here). The scene is DRAW-CALL bound: 12,474 meshes (only 800k tris total, so
not GPU/fill bound; it's per-object CPU overhead). Lowering pixel ratio did
nothing (confirms not fill-bound); shadows were ~20% of the frame.

Fixes (safe, no visible artifacts, measured ~24.5ms after):
- Shadow frustum ±95m -> ±58m, biased toward travel direction. The shadow pass
  is draw-call bound, and the old frustum drew thousands of distant scenery
  casters for shadows you can't see. Tightening culls them by distance while
  keeping foreground + car shadows — and the same 2048 map over a smaller area
  makes near shadows SHARPER.
- Removed preserveDrawingBuffer (nothing reads the backbuffer — realm
  thumbnails are static JPGs), letting the browser optimize buffer swaps.

Remaining lever (not in this commit): the 12k scenery draw calls are the root
cost of the camera pass; batching/instancing them is the path to a locked 60,
but it's a larger, look-sensitive change worth its own careful pass.

Batch scenery per-prop: halve the draw calls, keep the lush look

The racing frame was CPU-bound on ~12,500 scenery draw calls. Each scenery prop
(tree, rock, mushroom, building) is a Group of 5-8 separate sub-meshes, one draw
call each.

mergeProp() collapses every freshly-built prop's sub-meshes into one mesh per
material, in the prop's LOCAL space. Local-space is the key: the foliage wind
shader keys its sway AMOUNT off local vertex height (transformed.y) and its
PHASE off world position (modelMatrix), so a per-prop local merge keeps both
intact — cross-prop world-space merging would have broken the sway. Materials
are deduped by signature and geometries bucketed by exact attribute set so a
merge can never mismatch; props with sprites/instanced/skinned/multi-material
parts are skipped, and any failure returns the original untouched — batching
never changes how a prop looks. Obstacle collision is unaffected (recorded by
position, independent of the visual mesh).

Measured on a forest race: meshes 12,474 -> 5,627, render cost ~24ms -> 11.75ms
(~33fps -> ~85fps in the same browser). Forest verified visually identical.

+field strings out by personality, rubber-banded so one bad lap doesn't end your day — but

+flat-out when you are. Big call-outs punch in for the moments that matter: **OVERTAKE!** (with
+the place you just took), **PASSED**, and **FINAL LAP**.

+gold/silver/bronze podium glow, your score and personal best, a one-tap rematch — with
+championship and leaderboard screens cut to match.

+
+## The engineering war-story — 33 → 85 fps
+
+It looked finished. It didn't *feel* finished — the driving wasn't smooth. So instead of
+guessing, I profiled it live in the running engine:
+
+- The **physics was free**: ~0.05 ms/frame. Game logic was never the problem.
+- The whole cost was **rendering**, and it was **draw-call bound** — the scene was **~12,500
+  separate meshes** (but only 800k triangles, which a GPU eats for breakfast). Dropping the
+  resolution did nothing; the cost was per-object CPU overhead.
+
+The scene was heavy because every prop — every tree, rock and building — was a little cluster
+of **5–8 sub-meshes**, one draw call apiece. Two fixes:
+
+1. **Tighter shadows.** The sun's shadow frustum was drawing thousands of *distant* objects
+   into the shadow map for shadows you can't even see. Shrinking it culls them by distance —
+   and, as a bonus, the same shadow map over a smaller area comes out *sharper*.
+2. **Batched scenery — in local space.** Each prop's sub-meshes now collapse into one mesh per
+   material. The subtle part: the foliage **wind shader keys its sway off local vertex
+   height**, so the merge had to happen in each prop's *own* space — a naïve world-space merge
+   would've made every tree flail. It's fully defensive: anything it can't safely batch it
+   leaves untouched, so it can never change how a prop looks.
+
+Result, measured on a forest race:
+
+| | before | after |
+|---|---|---|
+| Meshes / draw calls | 12,474 | **5,627** |
+| Render time | ~24–30 ms | **11.75 ms** |
+| Effective FPS | ~33 | **~85** |
+
+Same lush forest, pixel-for-pixel — **2.5× the framerate**.

Fun arcade UI overhaul + real PBR roughness and an HDR environment probe

INTERFACE (HomeScreen / ResultsScreen / GameApp / globals.css)
Full redesign of the non-race UI toward a fun arcade feel: "INSERT COIN -
PRESS START" marquee, chunky display title, numbered realm chips over the
preview art, a glowing step rail with checkmarks, summary chips with SWAP,
per-realm lore, a lap selector, a big gradient START RACE button, and a
"HALL OF LEGENDS" leaderboard. CSS-only motion with a prefers-reduced-motion
guard; no new dependencies. All existing contracts preserved (GameOptions,
onFinish/GameResult, name persistence, leaderboard read/write).

GRAPHICS — realism
1. Real per-texel roughness. Downloaded the matching CC0 Poly Haven ARM maps
   (AO/Roughness/Metalness packed, glTF convention) for all 8 texture sets we
   already ship, and wired roughnessMap through the loader, tileSet, the road
   and every ground/rock/bark/foliage material. 2,344 meshes now vary their
   roughness per texel instead of sharing one flat constant, so wet patches,
   worn asphalt and damp bark catch light differently.
   The road pre-divides by the map's ~0.8 mean (roughness = f.rough / 0.8) so
   each realm keeps its intended wet/dry/ice finish instead of being silently
   glossed up ~20%.
2. Real HDR environment probe. makeEnvMap was a 256x128 sRGB canvas, which
   clamps at white — so nothing could ever throw a hot specular glint and car
   paint/metal/wet tarmac all read as flat plastic. Replaced with a 512x256
   Float32 equirect probe carrying a sun at ~30x white, matched to the scene's
   key-light elevation. PMREM now has real range and detail to work with.

Costs nothing: measured 8.03 ms/frame after (baseline was ~11.75 ms), 83
textures. Typecheck clean, production build clean.

Rebuild the engine sound: it was literally a mosquito

The old engine was two bare sawtooths a perfect FIFTH apart, swept
monotonically from 46 Hz to 196 Hz with a lowpass opening to 2100 Hz. A pure
tone rising without end is, precisely, the sound a mosquito makes — and there
was no noise component and no firing pulses at all, so it could never read as
a machine.

Four fixes:

1. GEARBOX. Six ratios: within a gear the revs sweep idle -> redline, and
   crossing into the next gear DROPS them back down, with a brief level dip so
   you hear the shift. That saw-tooth rev profile is the strongest "this is a
   car" cue there is, and it's what kills the endless rise. Measured 5 shifts
   across the speed range.
2. PITCH. Fundamental held low (54.9-113.5 Hz, was 46->196), with a sine sub an
   octave under for weight, and the second oscillator moved to the OCTAVE
   instead of that ringing bare fifth.
3. AIR. A looped brown-noise bed through a resonant bandpass that tracks revs
   and opens up on boost. Real engines are mostly moving air; this was missing
   entirely, which is why only the oscillators were audible.
4. CHUG. An LFO at the firing rate amplitude-modulates the tone stack — deep and
   lopey at low rpm, smoothing out as it spins up, like a real engine losing its
   lumpiness. Brightness ceiling cut from 2100 Hz to ~1400 Hz.

Measured A/B on the same graph at identical speed (analyser on the engine bus):
  spectral centroid      837 Hz -> 551 Hz   (-34%)
  energy above 1.2 kHz    23.1% -> 13.1%    (-43%)

Engine sound pass 2: real harmonic spectrum, exhaust formants, throttle response

The gearbox fixed the PITCH; the timbre was still synthetic. Three things were
still missing, and one was actively wrong.

1. WAVEFORM. Sawtooths roll their harmonics off as a plain 1/n — the classic
   synth buzz that no amount of filtering makes combust. Replaced with a custom
   PeriodicWave stating an engine-like spectrum directly: strong fundamental and
   2nd, a dip in the 3rd, pronounced EVEN harmonics above that. That even-harmonic
   emphasis is what reads as a growl.
2. EXHAUST FORMANTS. Three fixed resonant peaks (body ~f0, growl 620 Hz, edge
   1500 Hz) instead of a bare lowpass. Filtering can shape brightness but never
   gives an instrument character; resonances do.
3. THROTTLE LOAD. setEngine now takes `load` (1 on power, 0.22 coasting, 0
   braking) from the game's real throttle state. A car's note changes completely
   between driving and trailing throttle — without it the sound could only ever
   be a function of speed, which is why it stayed synthetic after the gearbox.
4. REV WANDER. A small bounded random walk on rpm, plus the two oscillator banks
   detuned 14 cents apart so they beat. A perfectly steady pitch is the giveaway.

Also corrected an over-correction: the first attempt at this pass measured
centroid 347 Hz with only 3 audible harmonics and near-zero throttle contrast —
i.e. muffled. Brightness is not the enemy once the fundamental sits at ~84 Hz
instead of 196: a mosquito is a thin high PURE TONE, whereas rich harmonics over
a LOW fundamental is a growl. So the filter now opens hard on the power.

Measured on the engine bus (driving setEngine at 60 Hz so smoothed load
converges — measuring it with a single call is how I initially fooled myself):
                 centroid   >1.2kHz   harmonics
  coasting        395 Hz      5.0%        4
  on throttle     505 Hz      9.0%        4
  nitro           661 Hz     15.5%        7
  => +110 Hz centroid swing between coasting and power.
For reference the original mosquito measured 837 Hz / 23.1% as a pure rising tone.

Graphics: real baked AO + 4096 shadows (both free), GTAO as an opt-in

BAKED AMBIENT OCCLUSION — free, and it was sitting unused. The ARM textures
already loaded for roughness carry baked AO in their RED channel, so contact
darkening in every crack and crevice costs nothing extra at render time. The
catch: three.js reads `aoMap` from the SECOND uv channel (`uv1`), which none of
our geometry has, so an assigned aoMap renders as literally nothing. Rather than
thread a second UV set through every builder, wireAmbientOcclusion() aliases
uv1 -> uv wherever a material actually uses an aoMap. 2344 meshes now have real
AO, 0 broken.

SHADOWS 2048 -> 4096, PCF radius 4 -> 7. Both measured essentially FREE
(2048 vs 4096: 11.05 vs 11.08 ms; radius 2 vs 10: 11.01 vs 11.47), because the
shadow pass is draw-call bound rather than pixel bound and the frustum is tight.
Texel density goes 5.7 cm -> 2.8 cm over the +-58 m frustum. This directly
contradicts the old "4096 costs 4x" note — that was measured against the WIDE
+-95 m frustum, before the batching work.

GTAO — resurrected from dead code into a real pause-menu toggle, but OFF by
default. It costs ~5.6 ms and a loaded forest view already sits at ~11 ms, so
enabling it puts the frame at 16.6 ms: exactly the 60 fps line with zero margin,
which is how you ship stutter to anyone on slower hardware. The baked AO above
now covers most of what it was for. Anyone with GPU headroom can switch it on.

Also corrected my own measurement error: an earlier 6.66 ms baseline (which made
GTAO look like it cost only 4.19 ms and fit comfortably) was taken from a light
view immediately after respawn. ~11 ms is the honest figure for a loaded view.

Shipped config: 11.23 ms/frame, ~89 fps, 5.37 ms of headroom.

F1-style 10-car grid from P10, longer laps, ramps back, film grade

GRID — 10 cars, and you always start P10. OPPONENT_COUNT 7 -> 9 (roster extended
to 10 names); the grid code already seated the player in the backmost slot, so
this gives an F1 staggered grid with you at the very back every race. Pace spread
tightened 0.10 -> 0.06: across ten cars a 0.10 spread left the tail at 0.90 of
your top speed, so the back half was free places — now the whole field sits
within 6% and passing all nine is a real climb.
Verified: 10 racers, 9 opponents, player start position 10, pole 1.0 / tail 0.94.

LONGER LAPS — new TRACK_SCALE (1.55) multiplies every realm's control points in
X/Z, stretching each circuit while preserving its shape, corner sequence and
elevation. Y is deliberately untouched, or the hills would become cliffs.
Everything downstream is expressed per-metre of arc length, so scenery, pickups,
terrain and the minimap all follow with no hand-retuning.
Verified: forest 1.56 km -> 2.41 km, ~40 s a lap, so a 3-lap race is ~2 min.

RAMPS ARE BACK, and this time they work. Two real defects:
  1. RAMP_SPECS claimed to be "single-lane" but was half-width 3.2-3.4, i.e.
     6.4-6.8 m on a 10 m road — two thirds of the track. You couldn't avoid one.
     Now half-width ~1.5 (one lane, ~3.3 m) with heights and launch power cut, so
     there is always a clear line past it.
  2. `this.ramps` — the array the ride-up physics iterates — was populated by
     NOTHING. Ramps were pure decoration you drove straight through. Now
     registered on spawn, with the half-length and the playerX lane conversion
     handled (addEntity places at lateral*5 while playerX divides by 4.5, so the
     collision band would otherwise sit off-centre from the visible ramp).
Verified: 7 ramps per lap, all 7 registered for physics.

NITRO trimmed 145 m -> 300 m spacing. Watch the trap: 200 m looked like a 31%
density cut but the 1.55x longer lap turned it into 24 cans per lap, MORE than
the 20 before. 300 m lands 16 per lap — an actual trim.

FILM GRADE — a new post pass placed AFTER OutputPass, i.e. on tone-mapped
display-space colour, because grain and chromatic aberration need a display
response curve; in linear HDR they misbehave. Gentle S-curve, cool-shadow /
warm-highlight split tone, slight saturation lift, fine animated grain, and
radial chromatic aberration that only bites at the frame edge.
Cost ~0.5 ms: frame 11.77 ms, ~85 fps.
