Ramps that work, random weather, and an endless NEON RUN mode

RAMPS — the reason they threw you off wasn't the ramps, it was three things:
  1. Air steering was hard-coded to 0 while airborne. The car keeps its world
     velocity, so on any bend the road curves away underneath you and you land in
     the scenery with NO way to influence it. Asphalt gives you air control for
     exactly this; now so do we (assist x1.25 in the air).
  2. Ramps were placed on a fixed stride regardless of corners. A ramp on a bend
     launches you along the tangent while the road turns away — unavoidable
     off-track. Placement now walks forward to find a genuinely straight section,
     and checks the WHOLE flight: at ~55 m/s a ramp is airborne ~1.3 s and lands
     ~72 m downrange, so a 70 m check let one land just past the straight. 110 m.
  3. Side-lane ramps measured as almost unhittable — the pure-pursuit steering
     assist constantly pulls you to the centreline, so it steers you OFF a ramp
     parked in lane 1 or 3 (2 of 4 never launched in testing). All ramps are now
     centre-lane; they're gentle and land you back on the road, so they're a
     feature you get to use rather than an obstacle.
Measured before/after: 2 of 4 launching -> 3 of 3 launching, 2 of 3 landing
clean and the third clipping the verge for 3 frames (0.05 s).

Instance the forest: 4x the trees at HALF the frame cost, plus real hills

THE UNLOCK. Every tree was its own Group of meshes, and because the renderer is
draw-call bound the tree count converted almost linearly into frame time — which
is why density kept having to be rationed (3 rows measured 10,518 meshes /
24.3 ms / 41 fps). Grass was always cheap for exactly one reason: it's instanced.
makeTreeField() now does the same for trees — build N distinct variants, then
draw every placement of a variant in ONE instanced call per material. Cost is
variants x 2 draw calls regardless of how many thousand trees exist.

So density stopped being a budget question:
  before  2 rows, stride 7.4  ->  8,161 meshes,  15.31 ms (65 fps)
  after   4 rows, stride 3.4  ->  6,372 meshes + 29 instanced calls, 7.26 ms
Roughly 4x the trees, and the frame HALVED. 103,822 instances now draw in 29
calls. Grass went with it (9k -> 34k lawn, 26k -> 60k understory) to kill the
barren ground, and it costs nothing.

Two things this had to get right:
- The wind shader derives sway PHASE from world position so neighbouring trees
  move out of step, but for an InstancedMesh modelMatrix is shared by every
  instance — so it now folds in instanceMatrix under #ifdef USE_INSTANCING.
  Without that the entire forest sways in perfect unison, reading as one giant
  object breathing.
- Variants bake their local geometry but deliberately NOT the group's random
  yaw; yaw is applied per instance, so 6 variants still give a forest where no
  two trees face the same way.
Only the innermost tree row registers as a collision obstacle now (2,644), since
the outer rows are too far back to be a hazard.

HILLS. The authored control points varied only ~6 m of height across a whole lap,
which is why circuits felt dead flat. Rather than re-author every realm by hand,
track.ts layers a two-octave hill profile over them, driven by position AROUND
THE LOOP and built only from whole-number sine harmonics so it's exactly periodic
— the seam meets at the same height AND slope, so the closed curve gets no step
or kink. Elevation range 6 -> 14.8 m at a max 5.1% grade: a drivable roll, not a
launch ramp. Measured 12.2% of a lap now has air time under the wheels.

through the shared faceRoad() helper and twice got it backwards, so you saw the
bare rear of a 74 x 42 m cliff with the water pouring away out of sight. The

Make the road curtain actually look like water

That white slab across the road was my water curtain, and it was indefensible:
untextured planes with an UNLIT MeshBasicMaterial, three of them stacked, so the
alphas composited into a solid opaque rectangle hanging in mid-air. A flat
untextured plane cannot read as water however transparent you make it — the eye
needs vertical STREAKS, and it needs the edges to DISSOLVE rather than stop at a
straight line. Transparency alone just gives you a translucent billboard.

Rebuilt so the alpha channel does the work: a generated 128x256 texture of
vertical streaks at varying brightness with fine grain so it doesn't band, its
alpha multiplied by sin(pi*u) across the width and ramped in at the top, so the
sheet has no rectangular border anywhere. Two layers at different repeats and
scroll speeds for parallax, scrolling downward each frame. Still no collision and
no shadow, so you punch straight through it.

Third attempt at this feature. For the record the other two: scaling
makeGrandWaterfall down dragged its 60 m cliff and plunge pool onto the
carriageway; then the untextured planes above. The lesson worth keeping is that
"make it transparent" is not the same as "make it look like water".

City-pop art direction, first cut: sunset sky, poster sun, silhouettes

Reference is Hiroshi Nagai / 80s Japanese city-pop: flat poster shapes, a hard
gradient sunset, one big clean sun disc, and near-black foreground silhouettes.

The key realisation is that this style is a LIGHTING problem, not a modelling
one. Nagai's foregrounds are dark because they're backlit — the sky is the light
source. So rather than restyle thousands of props, this makes the sky hot and
drops the ambient, and the existing geometry falls into silhouette by itself:

- Forest sky is now a violet -> magenta -> coral -> amber sunset ramp, with fog
  recoloured to a warm 0xd96a63 and pushed out (840 -> 1250) so the distance
  melts into the sky instead of ending in a green haze.
- hemiInt 0.98 -> 0.42 and a warm sun. Low ambient is the whole point: unlit
  faces go black against a bright sky, which is what makes a silhouette read.
- New `posterSun` palette flag draws a big HARD-EDGED disc just above the
  horizon with a broad bloom around it. The existing sky deliberately avoided a
  disc (a hard sun in the wrong place reads as a bug); this opts in per realm,
  because the flat circle IS the signature of the look.

Applied to the forest only so far — the other seven realms keep their current
palettes until the direction is confirmed.

1. THE PAINT WASHED OUT. carPaint is physically correct, and that's exactly the
   problem here: poster realms run a very low ambient (hemiInt 0.40) so scenery
   falls into silhouette, and a correct PBR car under that light goes dark and
   grey. But in the reference art the car is the one BOLD saturated shape in the
   frame — it holds its colour regardless of how much light reaches it. New
   setCarPosterMode() gives the paint an emissive floor of its own colour,
   flattens the clearcoat and drops metalness, so the livery survives the
   lighting instead of being at its mercy. Engine turns it on for any realm
   flagged posterSun.

2. WRONG SILHOUETTE. The screenshots I'd been judging by were the dragster and
   the F1 — huge exposed slicks and wings, the opposite of a road supercar seen
   from behind. Retuned the GT coupe to genuine supercar proportions: longer
   (4.3 -> 4.72), wider (1.96 -> 2.06), much lower (ride 0.9 -> 0.62) with a
   shallower canopy (0.34 -> 0.26), so from behind it reads as a low wedge with
   covered wheels rather than a kart.

THE WALL ACROSS THE ROAD was a variable I overloaded. `coast.r` started life as
the island radius and I later repurposed it as the causeway half-width (34 m)
without updating the skyline placement, which multiplies it: 34 * 2.15 = 73 m
from the circuit centre, i.e. towers standing ON the track. Now split into two
named fields — `r` (how far land extends either side of the tarmac) and `far`
(the circuit's own radius, used to push the far shore out). Measured after:
nearest skyline mesh is 265 m from the racing line.

THE "DIABOLICAL" CLOSE-UP was the HOOD camera. It sits `back: 2` — two metres
BEHIND the car's centre — which was fine over the old tall kart but ends up
inside the new low supercar body, giving a full-screen shot of the driver's
helmet. A bonnet cam belongs ahead of the centre, so back: -1.6 with a lower eye
line: nothing of the car is between you and the road now.

PALMS were placed at ROAD_HALF_WIDTH + 5, close enough for a trunk to overhang
the tarmac on a bend — which is why they read as standing on the road — and they
had no collision at all, so you drove through them. Now +12 m minimum and
registered as solid obstacles (2,145 on the lap).

interruption; the weather is visible, it doesn't need narrating over the racing.

Replace the kart grid with a supercar catalogue; unblur the sky

THE SKY. Two separate faults, one of them a real bug.

The cloud deck was generated at a QUARTER of the dome resolution (512x256)
and upscaled 4x with smoothing onto the largest surface on screen, so every
cloud edge was four pixels of interpolation. It's now generated at half
resolution, and for poster realms the alpha ramp is quantised into three
steps and the shading into two, because the 80s city-pop reference paints
clouds as flat cut shapes — a soft gradient is what makes a stylised sky look
like a low-res photo of nothing.

The bug: the clouds were baked into the same texture as the sun and the
gradient, so they could never move — a sky that never moves is a painted
backdrop. They now ride their own dome that rotates (a revolution every ~12
minutes). Getting that wrong the first time is worth recording: a transparent
mesh is drawn in the transparent pass, i.e. after every opaque object, and
renderOrder only sorts it WITHIN that pass. With depthTest off the dome
painted its cloud texture straight over the cars, the palms and the gantry —
the sky was literally on top of the world.

THE CARS. All ten are real-road-car archetypes now, built by one
parameterised builder instead of ten hand-written ones, because what actually
distinguishes an F40 from a 240Z is proportion plus five or six appendages —
everything else is the same lofted monocoque. Sharing it means a fix to the
shoulder line or the tail lands on the whole grid at once, which is exactly
what the ten separate builders stopped doing.

  F40 (red, straked wing, pop-ups, NACA ducts, quad round lamps, triple pipe)
  MERIDIAN (centre-seat, roof snorkel), VELOCE (two-tone quad-turbo),
  TAURO (basket-handle wing), TESTA (five side strakes, slatted tail),
  ZANZA (glass canopy), IMPREZ (rally sedan, blade wing, bonnet scoop),
  FIREHAWK (whale tail, shaker scoop), IROC (four round lamps, ducktail),
  FAIRLADY (long-bonnet fastback, chrome bumpers)

Wheels were at 0.80 of the half-width, which buried them INSIDE the bodywork:
the flank is a flat wall held at full width up to the shoulder, so a tyre
inboard of it is simply invisible. They now stand slightly proud, with a dark
arch liner and a body-colour eyebrow so the flank reads as cut away.

Tail lamps sat a few cm inside the kamm face and were half-swallowed by it;
they're now proud of it, hotter, and let into a dark panel.

Also from the report: palms were pink (0.29 base vertex tint under a 0xffb27a
hemisphere comes back as salmon, not silhouette) and up to 18 m tall — now
dark and 6-9 m. Roadside reflector caps were an UNLIT material multiplied by
0.42, i.e. permanently dark: a black ball on a white post. Beach clutter was
34k tufts of near-black scrub scattered 150 m over a 6 m strip of sand; now
sparse bleached dune grass on the strip only.

Fix the wheel-arch hoops, shallow cabins and unreadable car names

Three faults the showroom made obvious that the chase camera never would:

The body-colour arch eyebrow I added with the wheels was a torus at the

Make the sky hard-edged, fix the lollipop lights, facet the cars

SKY. Resolution was never the problem. A continuous gradient has no edges in
it, and a surface with no edges reads as out of focus however many pixels you
give it — which is why bumping the dome didn't fix "the sky is blurry".

  - the sky above the horizon is now QUANTISED into 16 flat bands, packed
    tighter toward the horizon where the colour moves fastest
  - poster realms drop the fBm cloud deck entirely. fBm gives a soft
    probability field; smoothstep its alpha and you have a gradient. Clouds
    are drawn as VECTORS instead — flat lozenges in three hard tones (lit top,
    mid band, shaded underside), at full dome size with no upscale step
  - the horizon haze is down to a quarter strength on poster realms, because
    it's a soft vertical wash laid exactly over the new band edges

One real trap in the vector clouds: the equirect wraps W texels around a
circle that shrinks toward the pole, so a puff of fixed canvas width covers
more and more azimuth as it climbs — at 60 degrees up the same ellipse smears
into a ribbon right across the sky. Width now scales down with elevation.

LIGHTS. The marker posts have been wrong twice in opposite directions: dark
stem + dark cap read as "small black pillars", so I brightened the cap — and
turned it into a glowing white SPHERE on a white stick, a row of lollipops
down both verges. A real marker post is a slim blade with a small flat
reflector PLATE facing the traffic, turned edge-on to the road. That's what it
builds now; the bright part is a 11 cm panel, not a ball.

CARS. Two causes of the smoothed look, both fixed: the body loft was
resampled 6x per section, which splines the creases out of existence (now 2),
and the paint used smooth vertex normals, which averages every remaining
crease away (now flat-shaded in poster realms). The shoulder line, the haunch
and the tail cut come back as hard edges with a tone step across them.

Six new maps from the reference photographs, with real elevation

  PORT AZUR    Riviera street circuit — 5 m on the harbour front to 38 m
               around the hill, barriers, apartment blocks, a 132 m tunnel
  HOKKAI PASS  snow pass — 4 m in the valley to 90 m at the saddle in one lap,
               plowed walls, black firs, avalanche galleries
  MIRAGE MILE  Gulf expressway — deliberately the flattest realm; the long
               rises exist to make the skyline move in the windscreen
  BASIN RUN    high desert — 12 m to 68 m twice a lap, so the road vanishes
               over a crest the way a desert highway does
  CAPE ROAD    clifftop coast — the biggest range of any realm at 15 m to
               117 m, with the Pacific up to 104 m below the outside verge
  SUNSET HILLS canyon switchbacks over a city at dusk — tightest radii here,
               30 m to 128 m of climb

Elevation is authored into the control points rather than left to the global
rolling-hill profile, and each realm's hillScale is turned down accordingly so
the two don't fight. "Ups and downs" is the whole character of a driving road;
a flat loop with scenery bolted on is a racetrack, not a drive.

The coastal machinery is now data rather than a hardcoded `realm.id === "bay"`
branch. A causeway and a clifftop road are the same system with different
numbers — land width, shore-band width, drop — so Cape Road gets a 14 m band
with a 150 m drop (a cliff) where Sunset Bay gets 9 m and 46 m (a beach).
Skyline and palms are flags on the same block.

Verified by driving a full lap of each under power, snapping back to the
centreline each step so the probe measures terrain rather than my driving:
every realm reports zero verge poking above the road surface, no road section
at or below its own waterline, and laps completing.

Palms needed two tint sets, not one. Under the near-black ambient of a sunset
realm anything above ~0.15 comes back salmon pink instead of silhouetted;
under a bright daylight hemisphere those same values are a dead grey-purple
stick. Lit realms now get an actual brown trunk and green crown.

Facet the terrain and unify the palms

Smooth vertex normals turn a heightfield into a soft rolling wash: the hills
have no edges in them, so they read as blurred layers rather than as land.
Poster realms now flat-shade the terrain — every slope gets its own flat tone
and a hard crease where slopes meet, which is what makes a hill look like a
hill in this art style — and drop to 9 m cells, since the facets are now the
look rather than just the sampling accuracy. The verge and the shore apron are
faceted to match; a smooth-shaded verge against a flat-shaded hillside shows
up as a soft seam running the length of the road.

And there were two different palms in the game. The scenery `palm` kind was
still the desert one, whose crown is flat trapezoids in dusty green — under a
sunset palette that arrives as an orange starfish on a stick, which is what
Sunset Hills was full of. Both now share the frond geometry: a rachis with 26
stations of leaflets combed off either side.

Find the actual cause of the blurry sky; fix the car's rear

THE SKY. I had been guessing. Dumping the live dome texture to a canvas and
looking at it showed the cause immediately: two radial gradients, 0.62 and
0.95 of the dome HEIGHT across, painted over the whole upper sky at 0.30 and
0.22 alpha, plus a third 6.5-radius halo around the sun disc. A soft white
bloom covering everything — and drawn AFTER the band quantisation, so it
erased the one thing meant to make the sky crisp. Naturalistic realms still
want it. A screen-printed sunset does not: the sun is a shape with a tight
ring and the sky around it is flat colour.

Clouds were all inside a 2-53 degree band hugging the horizon, where they
overlapped into a solid smear, leaving the zenith bare. They now run from just
off the horizon to overhead, at a third of the size and three times the count,
with density peaking at mid elevation — at 2 degrees up you are looking
through 30 km of cloud deck, which is why packing that row produced haze
rather than clouds. Each one is a proper cumulus: a FLAT BASE with circular
lobes on top. That flat bottom is the whole silhouette, and a cloud built from
a row of ellipses is lumpy on both sides and reads as a smudge.

Bands are now even in elevation angle. The previous pow(t, 0.68) made them
widest at the zenith, where an equirect's latitude circles converge, so they
came out as concentric rings around the pole like a target; and banding now
stops before the top 18%, because nothing hides pole convergence except not
drawing an edge there.

THE CAR. The glitch on the back was z-fighting: the dark lamp panel sat at
-hl * 0.998 with a 0.03 depth, straddling the body's own rear face, leaving
two surfaces a hundredth of a metre apart. The diffuser's rear face was half a
millimetre off the same plane. Both moved clear.

Compute the poster sky instead of painting it

Fourth report of a blurry sky, so I stopped adjusting the art and measured the
pipeline. The dome is a 2048-wide equirect. The camera sees 72 degrees of it —
20%, or 410 texels — and stretches those across a 2560-pixel device buffer. A
6x magnification. Mipmaps were on with anisotropy 1 on top of that, so near
the horizon the GPU chose its LOD from the long axis of a very stretched texel
footprint and blurred the sharp axis to match. Nothing drawn into that canvas
could ever have arrived sharp, and matching the screen with texels would take
a dome about 12,000 px wide — half a gigabyte of texture.

So the poster sky is analytic now. Gradient, band steps and the sun's edge are
evaluated per fragment on the dome, which means there is no resolution
involved at all and every edge is exactly as crisp as the display. The sun
disc is anti-aliased across one pixel using the screen-space derivative, so it
is hard without stair-stepping. The top fifth stays smooth because an
equirect's latitude lines converge at the pole and a hard edge up there reads
as rings around a target.

Clouds stay a texture — shapes that irregular aren't worth an SDF — but at
4096 with the mip chain off, linear filtering and anisotropy 16. There is
nothing to alias on a dome that is always magnified and never minified.

One trap worth recording: a raw ShaderMaterial does NOT inherit three's output
stages. Writing linear colour straight to gl_FragColor puts it on screen
un-encoded, and 0.023 linear displayed as sRGB is black — which is what the
zenith became. It needs <tonemapping_fragment> and <colorspace_fragment>
appended, exactly as every built-in material does.

Realms with stars or moons keep the canvas dome; that is where those are drawn.

Make the sky smooth again, and give the clouds volume

I conflated "sharp" with "posterised" and took your earlier note about
smoothened 3D effects too far. The result was a striped sky and clouds drawn
as flat filled shapes — paper cut-outs pasted on a gradient made of steps.
Neither is what a sky looks like, and you were right to call it.

The analytic dome was still the correct call: it is why the sky can be sharp
at all, since a 2048 equirect gives the camera 410 texels to cover 2560
pixels. But a shader has no banding to hide, so the gradient runs continuous
now — no quantisation at all.

The clouds are a noise field projected onto a deck overhead, which gives real
perspective for free: the same noise compresses toward the horizon exactly the
way a cloud layer does, instead of being pasted on at a fixed size. A second
sample stepped TOWARD the sun does the shading — where density falls off that
way the cloud faces the light, where it rises it is in its own shadow. That
cheap self-shadowing is the whole reason they read as solid rather than as cut
paper. They drift on a uTime uniform, so the separate 4096 cloud dome and its
draw call are gone.

Two things the first attempt got wrong and this one fixes: at a deck scale of
0.55 a single noise cell spanned 61 degrees of sky directly overhead (a flat
deck collapses to a point at the zenith), which is why the top of the sky was
one giant smear; and full-detail noise near the horizon is sub-pixel and
crawls, so the fine octaves now fade out with distance.

causeway; on Cape Road it laid a 50 m strip of beach along the top of a 150 m

Rebuild the mirrors, and merge the static car parts

Both of the things I flagged with the detail pass.

MIRRORS. The first version was a stick with a block on it, which at speed
reads as a red peg bolted to the door. A real wing mirror is a rounded housing
on a short arm raking up and out, with the glass set into its trailing face.
So: a tapered arm, a housing from a scaled sphere — round in plan, flattened
in section, which is the actual shape — and a glass panel angled back toward
where the driver's eyes are.

MERGING. The detail pass took a car from ~130 meshes to 167, and across a
ten-car grid that is 1,670 objects to cull and sort every frame, on a renderer
that has been draw-call bound before. None of that detail moves relative to
the shell, so it does not need to be separate objects — a mirror housing and a
diffuser fin in the same paint can share one buffer. Static parts are now
collapsed per material at build time: 167 meshes per car down to 108, with the
remainder being the four wheels (which spin and steer, so they are excluded)
and whatever is a lone user of its material.

The merge strips any attribute the set does not share and synthesises UVs
where a primitive lacks them, because mergeGeometries refuses a mismatched
set — a real risk here with a UV-mapped lofted body sitting next to boxes and
spheres. It falls back to leaving a material's meshes alone rather than
throwing, so a future part that cannot merge degrades instead of breaking.

Verified the car is visually unchanged after merging: body, wing, intakes,
louvres, lamps, brakes and mirrors all still present from three angles.

+# Fantasy Racer — what's left before this is public
+
+Written 2026-09-13. This is the honest list, not a wish list. Everything here
+is something that will bite when real people hit it, ordered by whether it
+*blocks* a public launch.
+
+Legend: **[BLOCKER]** must be done first · **[SHIP-SOON]** days after launch is
+fine · **[LATER]** real work, not urgent.
+
+---
+
+## 1. Data and persistence
+
+### [BLOCKER] The leaderboard is a lie across devices
+`src/ui/leaderboard.ts` keeps scores in `localStorage`. The home screen shows a
+**GLOBAL** tab next to **THIS DEVICE**, and Global currently shows the same
+local data. The moment two people compare scores, that's an obvious bug.
+
+Either wire up a real store or remove the Global tab before launch. A real
+store needs:
+
+- **Database.** Postgres is the default choice on Vercel (Neon/Supabase both
+  fine). One table is enough to start:
+  `scores(id, name, car, realm, mode, laps, time_ms, score, created_at)`.
+- **Write path.** `app/api/scores/route.ts` already exists as a stub — it needs
+  a real `POST` that validates and inserts, and a `GET` that returns a top-N
+  per (realm, mode).
+- **Anti-cheat, at least token effort.** The client currently computes the
+  score and would POST whatever it likes. Minimum viable: rate-limit by IP,
+  cap implausible values (a lap time below the theoretical minimum for the
+  car/realm, a score above what the pickup count allows), and reject
+  mismatched (time, score, laps) triples. Anything stronger means running the
+  sim server-side, which is not worth it for this.
+- **Name moderation.** Free-text names go on a public board. A blocklist and a
+  length cap at minimum.
+
+### [BLOCKER] No privacy notice, and we store a name
+Even a localStorage-only build stores a user-entered name. If the leaderboard
+goes server-side that's personal data leaving the device. Needs a one-page
+privacy note and a line on the name entry saying the name will be public.
+
+### [SHIP-SOON] No migration for saved data
+`fantasy-racer-car` in localStorage holds a `CarId`. The car IDs were renamed
+wholesale (`comet` → `f40` etc.) and the realm IDs have grown. An old visitor
+gets `CAR_SPECS[undefined]`. There's a guard on the car read but the saved
+*scores* still carry dead realm/car IDs and will render blank. Add a version
+key and drop or remap old entries.
+
+---
+
+## 2. Correctness and robustness
+
+### [BLOCKER] No error boundary
+If `Game.init()` throws — a bad GLTF, a WebGL context failure, an out-of-memory
+on a weak GPU — the canvas is black and nothing tells the user. Needs a React
+error boundary around `GameCanvas` and a "something broke, back to menu"
+screen.
+
+### [BLOCKER] No WebGL capability check
+The engine assumes WebGL2, float render targets, and a working PMREM. On
+hardware without them it fails silently. Detect up front and show a plain
+message instead of a black screen.
+
+### [SHIP-SOON] Unbounded memory across races
+Each race builds a new `Game`, new textures, new geometry. `stop()` exists but
+I have not audited that every texture/geometry/material is disposed. Play
+twenty races in one session and find out. Needs a leak test: race → menu →
+race ×20, watching `renderer.info.memory`.
+
+### [SHIP-SOON] The dev-only preview writer ships in the bundle
+`app/api/devpreview/route.ts` writes files to disk. It refuses when
+`NODE_ENV === "production"`, which is correct on Vercel, but it should not be
+in the production bundle at all. Move it behind a build-time exclusion or
+delete it and regenerate previews locally when needed.
+
+---
+
+## 3. Performance
+
+### [BLOCKER] No performance floor established
+Everything has been tuned on one machine. There is no data on a mid-range
+laptop, an integrated GPU, or a phone. Before launch: measure median frame
+time on at least a low-end integrated GPU, and add a quality toggle (shadow
+resolution, scenery density, the radial blur, bloom) that a user can drop.
+
+Known heavy spots, in order: scenery draw calls, the GTAO pass (off by
+default — keep it off), shadow map size, and now 108 meshes × 10 cars.
+
+### [SHIP-SOON] No frame-time telemetry
+There is no way to know whether real users are getting 60 fps. A simple
+opt-in counter posted with the score would answer it.
+
+### [LATER] Mobile is unhandled
+Touch controls do not exist, the HUD is laid out for a wide viewport, and the
+texture budget assumes desktop VRAM. Either commit to mobile properly or
+detect and tell the user it's desktop-only.
+
+---
+
+## 4. Audio
+
+### [BLOCKER] Music is not licensed
+Whatever is playing needs to be either original, CC0, or properly licensed,
+with attribution recorded. This is the single easiest thing to get sued over.
+Same audit for every model and texture: `public/models/LICENSE-*` covers the
+Kenney assets, but the PBR textures in `public/textures/` need their source
+and licence written down in the repo.
+
+### [SHIP-SOON] No audio autoplay handling
+Browsers block audio until a user gesture. If the first race starts silent
+there is no recovery and no prompt.

Cut the mode list, rebuild Neon Run, ease the speed, redo the home flow

MODES. Time Trial and Nitro Sprint are off the picker and Transformer Rush is
archived. All three remain in GameMode and MODE_CONFIG so saved scores and
direct calls still resolve — they are just not offered. Four strong modes read
better than seven where three are thin variations of one.

NEON RUN. It was a normal circuit with laps set to 9999, which is the problem:
a 3 km lap with corners is a RACE TRACK, and driving one forever with no
rivals just makes it an empty race track. It has its own world now, selected
automatically the way Space Wars selects its battle tube. Still a closed loop,
because the whole engine is built on one — but shaped so you never feel it:
two 5.3 km straights joined by sweepers wide enough that you barely turn the
wheel, 16 km a lap, so a straight lasts the better part of a minute. Night,
wet asphalt carrying the reflections, magenta and cyan kerbs, towers marching
down both sides. No ramps, because being thrown in the air every few hundred
metres is the opposite of a cruise. No minimap either — it is useless without
rivals, and worse, it draws the loop, which is the one thing the realm is
shaped to hide.

LIGHTING. makeStreetlight is a 4-5 m urban pole with a 1 m gooseneck: beside
the road and barely above a car's roof, so from the seat it reads as a small
bar on the verge. Motorway lighting is 10-12 m up with a 5-6 m reach, so the
lamps pass over your head — and that overhead rhythm is most of what makes a
night highway look like one. makeOverheadLight does that, with a lit lens on
the underside and a soft cone beneath it so the lamp reads as lighting
something rather than as a lit object.

SPEED. At 190 mph the roadside is a stroboscope: every post and tree crosses
the frame in two or three frames and, because nothing smears, each one is a
separate hard-edged flash. Things do not zip past so much as TELEPORT. A
radial blur pass now smears the periphery along the direction of travel — six
taps, strength from speed, falling to zero well before the middle of the
frame, so the road you are aiming at stays sharp. The FOV kick came down from
9/12 to 5/8 (a wide lens at speed stretches the periphery, which makes the
same object cross faster AND arrive distorted), and the 2D streak overlay
halved, since hard streaks on top of a blurred periphery is noise over noise.

HOME. The flow had two dead ends I kept walking into myself: NEXT sat disabled
until you explicitly clicked a car that was already selected and shown as
selected, and START refused until you typed a name. Both are gone — everything
is pre-picked, the name defaults, and every step is reachable. Added DRIVE NOW
at the top, which starts a race on the current selection in one click: four
steps is right for someone who wants to choose and three too many for someone
who wants to play.

Fix the sky dome escaping the camera, and take Neo-Tokyo seriously

THE SHAPE IN THE CORNER, AND THE MONO SKY — one bug, not two.

The sky dome is a radius-900 BackSide sphere sitting at the WORLD ORIGIN. That
is fine for a lap that fits inside it, which every realm did until now. The
Neon Run stadium spans 7 km, so you drive straight out through the wall — and
from outside, a BackSide sphere is invisible. The sky simply stops being
drawn: what fills the frame is the flat clear colour, and the dome's rim cuts
that dark arc across the corner. Measuring found it: hiding the dome changed
the sampled sky pixel by nothing at all, which it could not do if the dome
were the thing being drawn there.

The dome (and its cloud deck) now follow the camera. That is a general fix —
any realm bigger than 900 m had this waiting.

The mountain ring was the other mass: an 11 km ring of 120 m peaks standing
over the skyline of a city. Neon gets a ring of cut-out skyline instead.

THE LAMPS were a flat-opacity cone, which renders as a solid cyan triangle
hanging in the air. A real beam is invisible except where it hits something.
They are vertex-darkened downward now and additively blended, with the pool
they throw on the tarmac — which is the part the eye actually reads as
lighting rather than as a lit object.

AGAINST THE REFERENCE. Akira's Neo-Tokyo runs on three things this did not
have: light that is always MOTIVATED (signs, streetlamps, headlights, never an
ambient wash), blacks kept crushed and dense rather than lifted, and cyan and
green against that black with one saturated red accent.

  - the horizon haze alpha RISES as a palette darkens, which is right for a
    hazy dusk and backwards for a night city: on a near-black sky it laid a
    wash over 40% of the dome, and since you mostly look near the horizon that
    wash WAS the sky. Dark palettes get a tight band on the rooftops instead.
  - the palette went from a flat mid-purple at every stop to near-black at the
    zenith falling to a dirty magenta of light pollution on the rooftops, with
    stars, low ambient, and the fog pulled in to 620 so the towers stack into
    layers instead of standing as one wall.
  - no cloud deck: fbm overcast on a near-black sky is grey smears with
    nothing lighting them.
  - signage, 120 of them along the lap. Towers with nothing but window squares
    give the eye nothing to read as a city, and the signs are the light source
    the reference keeps insisting on.

Let the signs light the city

A sign that only lights itself is a sticker on a black wall. In the reference
a sign across the street puts its colour on the block opposite and on the wet
road underneath, and that spill is most of what makes the city read as LIT
rather than as decorated — the towers were unlit dark masses with lit windows
punched into them.

Each sign now throws three washes: onto the wall it is bolted to, onto the
road below it (stretched along the carriageway the way a real throw is), and
onto the block across the road, facing back the way the sign does.

They are radial falloffs, not flat quads. The old halo was a rectangle of
0.16 opacity, and a rectangle of even colour blended additively onto a wall
reads as exactly that — the same mistake the lamp cones made. One shared
texture supplies the falloff and the colour rides on the vertices, so every
wash in the realm shares a single material.

Sign density went from 120 to 260, which over a 16 km lap is one every 60 m
rather than every 133; at the lower count there were long dark stretches
between them.

The 520 road and far-block washes are merged into ONE mesh. They share a
material and never move, and this renderer is draw-call bound — 520 extra
objects to cull and submit is the exact shape of problem that has hurt it
before. Scene children: 1485 down to 966, with an identical render.

Stop the terrain cutting the road, and give the new circuits a shape

THE SLAB ACROSS THE CARRIAGEWAY. Not a shadow — the ground mesh chording over
the road. The terrain is a 12 m grid sampling the same height field, so
between two grid points it draws a straight line while the road keeps curving;
where the road sits in a dip, that chord passes OVER it. Measured on Cape
Road: 0.905 m of sag against a flat 0.12 m clearance, so the ground could
stand three quarters of a metre proud of the tarmac. The steeper elevation I
added last time is what made it show.

A constant big enough for the worst dip would dish the verge along the whole
lap, so the clearance is per-sample now: the road's own local sag over a 12 m
span, computed once into the terrain sample cache and smeared to its
neighbours so the dish eases in rather than stepping. Zero on the straights,
opening only where it has to.

ALL THE NEW MAPS WERE RINGS. Measurable, not a matter of taste — min/max
radius ratio (1.00 = a perfect circle): the six photo realms ran 0.66 to 0.82
on 24-28 control points, where the hand-authored originals are 0.15 to 0.37 on
50-66. Cape was 0.82. They were smooth rings with corners of one radius.

Regenerated on a polar r(theta) with harmonics — which guarantees a simple
closed loop while letting the shape be pushed hard, so radius can vary by a
factor of three without any risk of the track crossing itself. 46 points each,
and they now run 0.36 to 0.55: real straights, corners of genuinely different
radii, and a couple of tight ones per lap.

And the elevation is SMOOTH now rather than abrupt. Height comes from low-order
harmonics authored into the control points, with the global hill ripple turned
off for these realms so the two do not stack — that stacking is where the tight
vertical curvature came from. Worst chord sag on Cape: 0.905 m down to 0.019 m,
while the range got BIGGER, 5 m to 115 m over the lap. Terrain-above-road across
the whole corridor measures 0 everywhere.

THE CAR WAS LITERALLY FLOATING. CAR_LIFT was 0.2, and makeWheel already places
each wheel centre at exactly its radius — so the tyre's contact patch sits at
the car's own origin, and that lift was a 20 cm gap between the tyres and the
tarmac. It is 0.05 now, which is just enough to absorb the suspension travel
below without ever pushing the contact patch through the road. Measured on
Crystal Peaks: the car now rides between 0 cm compressed and 10 cm extended,
and it MOVES with the road instead of hovering at a constant height.

THE ELEVATION IS BACK, BIGGER. I smoothed it away to stop the terrain cutting
the road, which fixed the symptom and threw out the thing that was good. The
actual fix was the clearance, so the profiles can be dramatic again: Cape 6 to
227 m, Hokkai 6 to 184, Hills 10 to 239 — up from a 110 m range at most.

Safe now because of two things. The clearance under the road is per-sample,
derived from the road's own local sag, so it opens exactly where a dip needs
it and nowhere else. And the ground grid went from 12 m cells to 8: the chord
error goes as the SQUARE of the cell, so that alone cuts it to 44%, for 2.25x
the vertices of one static mesh. Terrain-above-road measures 0 across the full
corridor on Cape, Forest and Peaks.

AND IT IS ACTUALLY ALL MAPS THIS TIME. It was not before — Forest measured 0
degrees of bank and 34 m of elevation while I was claiming otherwise. Every
ground realm now has banking, off-camber and real undulation; the global hill

hillScale on top (Peaks 2.8, Forest 2.4, down to 0.8 for the grand-prix
stadium, which is graded flat on purpose). Void and Nebula stay out — they are

    placed at the FLAT centreline height so a tilted surface rose through it.
    It now reads the banked surface at the car's actual lateral offset. BANK_K

  - OFF-CAMBER. A circuit where every corner leans into you has one kind of
    corner. A slow harmonic inverts the bank over a few stretches a lap, so
    some bends fall away from the apex — smoothly, because a step change in

+procedurally in `src/game3d/cars.ts` from lofted sections. The Kenney car kit

+# Fantasy Racer — environment
+#
+# Every one of these is OPTIONAL. With none of them set the game runs fully:
+# scores go to localStorage, guests get a local number, nothing is reported.
+# Each one turns on a feature and says so honestly in the UI when it is off.
+#
+# Copy to .env.local for development. On Vercel, set them in
+# Project → Settings → Environment Variables (and redeploy — env vars are
+# baked into the client bundle at build time, not read at runtime).
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Shared leaderboard + the guest number sequence
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Without these, /api/scores keeps scores in per-instance memory — which on
+# serverless means they effectively vanish — and the GLOBAL tab says "shared
+# board activates once a KV store is connected". Guests get a random local
+# number instead of the next one in a real sequence.
+#
+# Easiest source: Vercel Marketplace → Upstash Redis (free tier is ample).
+# Adding it from the Vercel dashboard sets these for you automatically.
+# The UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_* pair is accepted as an alias.
+KV_REST_API_URL=
+KV_REST_API_TOKEN=
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Sign-in with Google  (optional; guest is always available)
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Google Identity Services, which needs only the PUBLIC client id — no secret,
+# no callback URL, no session store. Create one at
+# console.cloud.google.com → APIs & Services → Credentials → OAuth client ID
+# → Web application, and add your deployment origin to "Authorised JavaScript
+# origins". Unset, the Google button on the sign-in gate is disabled and says
+# it is not configured.
+NEXT_PUBLIC_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Crash reporting  (optional)
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# A Sentry DSN. It is a public credential — it is meant to ship in the client
+# bundle. See src/ui/report.ts: this posts the ingest envelope directly rather
+# than pulling in the ~90 kB Sentry SDK. Unset, crashes only reach the console.
+# Reports carry the error, the stack, the realm/mode/car and the GPU string.
+# They never carry a player name.
+NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN=
+
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Dev only
+# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
+# Lets /api/devpreview write realm preview JPEGs into public/previews. Refuses
+# to run in production regardless. Only set this while regenerating previews.
+FR_ALLOW_PREVIEW_WRITE=

+"use client";
+
+import { useEffect } from "react";
+
+/**
+ * Registers the service worker in production only.
+ *
+ * Dev is excluded deliberately: a worker intercepting requests in front of
+ * Next's dev server produces failures that look like code bugs and are not,
+ * and HMR and the worker's cache disagree constantly.
+ *
+ * Registration failing is not an error worth showing anyone — it means no
+ * offline support, and the game works fine without it.
+ */
+export default function ServiceWorkerRegister() {
+  useEffect(() => {
+    if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production") return;
+    if (!("serviceWorker" in navigator)) return;
+    // After load, so registration never competes with the first render for
+    // bandwidth on the one thing that matters — getting the game on screen.
+    const register = () => {
+      navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js").catch(() => {});
+    };
+    if (document.readyState === "complete") register();
+    else {
+      window.addEventListener("load", register);
+      return () => window.removeEventListener("load", register);
+    }
+  }, []);
+
+  return null;
+}

+Rebuilt around the Nagai/city-pop reference images: sunset gradients, poster
+suns, silhouetted skylines, flat-faceted geometry.

+  fix "blurry" because the blur was *magnification*, not drawing: the camera
+  sees ~72° of a 2048-px equirect, i.e. 410 texels stretched across a 2560-px
+  buffer — 6×. It is now a `ShaderMaterial`: continuous gradient, hard sun disc
+  anti-aliased by `fwidth`, and clouds as an fbm field projected onto a deck

Rename the game to Duskline

Fantasy Racer described a kart game that no longer exists — twelve
worlds, ten road cars and a sunset art direction are not "fantasy", and
"Racer" is unsearchable. Duskline is the sunset plus the racing line, and
it collides with nothing published.

Renamed: page title, share tags, PWA manifest, the wordmark on screen,
package name, the console/report prefix, the service-worker cache
version, the KV key prefixes, and every document.

SAVED DATA IS MIGRATED, NOT DROPPED. Everything the game stores was
prefixed fantasy-racer-, and renaming without handling that would
silently wipe every returning player's car, scores, settings and
identity — they would come back to a fresh install with no explanation.
src/ui/storage.ts is now the only place localStorage is touched, and the
migration is lazy rather than a startup pass: a read misses the new key,
finds the old one, adopts it, deletes the old. No ordering problem, no
flag, idempotent, and it costs nothing for a player who never returns.

schema migrate on the home screen, settings and mute on the first race,
and afterwards no fantasy-racer-* key remains. The saved quality tier
survived, the saved car (TESTA) came back selected, and the returning
player was not shown the sign-in gate.

home screen, and did not mention storage, identity, reporting or the
capability gate.

Collapse the city: 21,151 meshes down to 4,971

Profiling the scene graph instead of guessing was the whole trick. Neon
Run held 21,151 meshes, 18,066 of them plain 24-vertex boxes — about a
hundred per tower across 176 towers. Most are culled, but every one of
them still costs a matrix update and a frustum test on the CPU every
frame, and this renderer has been draw-call bound before.

mergeStaticParts already existed for cars (167 -> 108 meshes each). It
moves to src/game3d/merge.ts and makeNeoTower now calls it, collapsing
each tower to about four meshes — one per material. Safe precisely
because nothing in a tower moves: merging ACROSS props is what broke the
wind sway the last time this was tried, and that constraint is now
written into the helper's doc comment rather than remembered.

  Neon Run scene meshes  21,151 -> 4,971
  Neon Run plain boxes   18,066 -> 1,787
  Neon Run draw calls     1,838 -> 843
  Sunset Bay draw calls     641 -> 433

Triangle counts unchanged, as they should be — the geometry is identical,

Photo mode: let people look at the thing

The art direction is the point of this game and there was no way to see
it. The chase camera sits behind the car at a fixed height and the HUD
covers the corners, so the one thing worth showing off was the one thing
you could not frame.

Pause -> PHOTO MODE freezes the simulation, hides the HUD, and puts the
camera on an orbit you steer: arrows orbit and raise, Z/X dolly, Q/E
lens, SPACE shutter, ESC back. It reuses the engine's own render path, so
the photograph is exactly the image the game draws rather than the output
of a second, divergent renderer. The capture renders and reads the canvas
in one synchronous block, because the drawing buffer is cleared on
composite and preserveDrawingBuffer would tax every frame of every race
for the sake of a screenshot. Files are named after what is in them.

One flaw found by READING the frame loop rather than running it: frame()
returns before render() while paused, so a paused-but-live camera would
have rendered exactly one frame and then sat there — which looks like
dead controls, not a frozen world. The loop now renders while composing
and still skips update(), so nothing moves while you compose.

Input gained a public holding() reader rather than the engine reaching
into its private key Set.

Verified: 1,241 composer passes while paused === true, camera responds to
held keys (yaw 2.3 -> 4.34), capture is a real 1423x1491 PNG with 1,725
of 2,304 sampled pixels lit, caption reads "Sunset Bay · IMPREZ" rather
than raw ids, and ESC returns to the pause menu with the HUD and the
chase FOV restored.

Put size budgets in CI, and prove they catch the regression

Two of the hardest-won wins here regress from a single innocuous line and
nothing in the build output complains:

  - first-load JS was 405 kB because GameApp imported GameCanvas
    statically, so all of three.js shipped to display a menu that renders
    no triangles. A dynamic() import took it to 126 kB.
  - textures were 12.1 MB before the WebP pass took them to 916 kB. One
    full-resolution PNG dropped into public/textures undoes it quietly.

npm run test:budget measures a real build and fails on either. CI runs it
AFTER next build, because it measures the build.

PROVEN, not assumed: reintroducing the exact regression — one static
`import { Game } from "@/src/game3d/engine"` in GameApp — took first-load
from 195 to 389 kB and the test failed naming both the likely cause and
the file to look in. Next's own output agreed (page 23 -> 293 kB). Then
reverted.

Two details worth knowing. The ceiling is pinned to THIS SCRIPT'S
measure (~195 kB), not the ~166 kB a browser reports or the figure next
build prints: it sums the deduped page+layout chunk sets at gzip 9 where
the CDN serves brotli and the browser loads only what the HTML
references. A regression detector only has to be consistent with itself.
And it refuses outright when .next holds a DEV build — those chunks are
unminified and unhashed, and measuring them reports ~3 MB, which looks
exactly like a catastrophe rather than like a mistake.

A draw-call budget would be better still, but that needs a GPU and CI has
none. These are pure file arithmetic, so they run anywhere.

Start the race behind the start line, and make the line visible

Three faults in the one shot everybody sees first — the grid.

THE FIELD STARTED PAST THE LINE. The grid formed up AT distance 0 with
every rival arrayed ahead, so each race opened with the whole pack
already over the start/finish line and the player sitting on it. It read
as joining a race in progress. The grid is entirely behind the line now:
pole's nose 7 m back, each row 8 m further, player at the rear.

Lap counting compensates rather than drifting: lapProgress starts at the
same negative offset, so it reaches a full lap exactly when the car
returns to the line instead of ~37 m early. Verified — grid slots at
-5.4 through -39, player 36.98 m behind the line of a 3862 m lap, its
world position matching its slot. Solo modes never call spawnOpponents,
so gridStart stays 0 and Neon Run still starts on the line (verified).

THE LINE LOOKED HALF-WIDTH. It was a flat PlaneGeometry dropped at one
point with one rotation, and the road is banked and curving — a flat
rectangle can only meet that surface along one line, so most of its width
sank under the tarmac. It was full width the whole time; you could not
see it.

It is a strip that follows the road now, and the vertex maths is COPIED
from buildRoadMesh rather than re-derived through pointAt(). That
distinction was the fix: my first attempt used pointAt and landed ~8 cm
UNDER the ribbon, which is invisible everywhere rather than visible in
half. Two further faults found by measuring rather than guessing — the
winding copied from the terrain grid gave normals averaging -0.98 in y
(the strip faced the underside of the road), and a 1 cm lift loses the
depth test entirely at 20+ m on a 1600 m far plane. 7 cm, wound upward.

THE BOARD was 54px monospace on a flat slab, hanging over the grid where
it is in frame for every countdown of every race. Now the wordmark in the
game's own display face with START · FINISH beneath it, chequer down the
sides rather than across the top and bottom (which had squeezed the type
into a letterbox), the realm's kerb colour as a hairline, and a backlit
panel gradient. The gantry also moved from 2 m past the line onto it, so
the sign marks the place laps actually tick.

Make the nitro bar show what nitro actually is

It was one continuous gradient with tick marks — a fuel gauge — for a
resource that is three discrete charges. Four consequences, all of which
made it read oddly:

1. It drew (charges + fill) / 3 as a single level, so a bar at 63% (one
   charge plus 0.9 of the next) offered exactly ONE boost — the same as a
   bar at 34%. Identical capability, completely different picture.
2. At zero charges with a nearly-complete fill it showed a third of
   itself lit and SPACE did nothing. A meter that looks loaded and
   refuses to fire is the worst thing it did.
3. Earning and holding were the same colour, so there was no way to tell
   a spendable charge from progress toward one.
4. Spending dropped the level instantly, so for the 2.2 s the boost was
   actually running the bar already showed what you would have
   afterwards. Nothing showed the burn, or the cooldown that makes a
   second press bounce.

Now one cell per charge. Solid cyan = spendable. The next cell fills as a
dim sliver while it earns, which reads as "not yet" at a glance. A live
boost drains its own cell in real time in orange, and the label says
BOOSTING — which is also the on-screen answer to "why won't it fire
again".

Verified by sampling the HUD canvas pixels in every state rather than by
eye: empty rgb(28,24,48), earning rgb(50,86,108), held rgb(79,211,245);
and across a boost, cell orange at 100%, half-drained at 50%, empty at 0
while the held charge beside it stays lit.

ALSO A DOCUMENTATION BUG, mine, found while reading the model: the
first-run card and the pause reference both said drifting refills nitro.
It does not. Drifting sets driftBoostT — an instant boost as you
straighten — while nitro charges come back on a ~14 s timer and from
cans. All three places now say what the code does, and the bar's empty
label is CHARGING rather than DRIFT TO CHARGE.

Give the circuit things to do, and something to beat

Five features, all of them things the game already had the parts for and
none of them new assets.

GHOST LAP. Your best lap, driving beside you, stored per realm in
track-space (distance along the lap, lateral, heading) rather than world
XYZ so it survives any change to the road art. Sampled by DISTANCE, not
time: the only question a replay ever asks is "where was I at this point
on the track", and distance-indexed that is an array index. It also makes
the delta readout exact — how long the best lap took to reach where you
are, minus how long you have taken — instead of dividing the gap by your
current speed, which reads 4.5 seconds down for a 36 m gap the moment you
brake (measured). Lap 1 runs from the grid and is never stored: a standing
lap is not comparable to a flying one.

STYLE CHAIN. Drift, near miss, overtake, stunt and pad chain all pay into
a pot that PENDS rather than scores. Let the fuse lapse cleanly and you
bank it at up to x6; touch anything and you lose the lot. Verified: nothing
moves the score while the chain is alive, a clean lapse banks the pot, and
a break costs the pot without touching the score.

DRIFT ZONES. Painted corners that pay for how much of them you spent
sideways. Where they go is MEASURED, not authored — twelve realms generate
their own circuits, so the zones are placed on each lap's own busiest
corners by percentile. A first pass used absolute curvature thresholds and
found exactly one zone on a whole circuit whose tightest hairpin was 0.0116:
the floor had silently replaced the percentile. The band itself is the
gauge, warming violet to amber as you fill it. It only fills on tarmac —
the grass is looser than asphalt by design, so a run wide onto the verge
filled it faster than a real drift did.

BOOST PAD CHAINS. Pads are back, in threes on the OUTSIDE of corner exits,
where taking them costs you the tight line. They were pulled for being a
conveyor belt, which was true of a pad you cannot miss: the deck was
8.5 m wide on a 10 m road and its hit band was FIVE metres either side, so
a pad by the kerb still fired when you drove down the middle. Now a lane's
width, with a lane's hit band, and the second and third decks extend the
surge rather than refresh it so committing to the whole chain is worth more
than clipping the first.

SLIPSTREAM. The hole in the air behind the car in front: strongest right
behind the gearbox, gone by 30 m, and it bleeds out slowly so pulling out
to pass keeps the speed you earned. Measured over a full lap in traffic it
averages +2.0% top speed, with the strong band on 3% of frames.

Also:

- The camera no longer shows the underside of the road on a descent. It was
  clamped to the TERRAIN, which is deliberately held below the road ribbon,
  so on a hill the clamp left it under the tarmac. Now clamped to the road
  surface itself via project() + pointAt(). 0 frames under the road over a
  5400-frame lap, was visible on every descent.
- The grid stagger had the wrong sign: slot 1 sat 1.6 m AHEAD of slot 0, so
  pole was not on pole, every row was ordered backwards, and the player
  started ninth of ten on a grid meant to put them last. One sign fixes all
  three.
- CLEAN LANE no longer fires inside a drift zone. The two were paying for
  opposite things in the same moment.
- Toasts no longer print through the middle of the callout. They were laid
  out by two independent magic numbers; the callout now exports where it is.
- A gem run is one counting line, not six. Six chips 3.5 m apart is six
  toasts in half a second into a four-slot stack, which pushed every line
  that meant something off the top.
- Anisotropy 16 on every procedural texture (road, checker, ground, cars).
  The road runs to the horizon at a grazing angle, which is exactly where
  filtering smears, and it was on 8 — the cars on 4.
- Ghost samples are rounded on the way out: 56 kB per realm of raw doubles
  would have been an eighth of the localStorage quota for precision no one
  can see.

Make the weather matter, let the pack tow, and give each circuit a crossing

WEATHER IS NOW A RACE CONDITION. It already rolled over mid-race and already
changed the sky; it just had no consequence, which made it scenery. Rain,
snow, sand and ash now take LATERAL GRIP away — 0.78 at the worst — and
nothing else. That is the interesting lever: the straights are unchanged,
every corner has to be taken slower or sideways, and since the drift
threshold is a side-slip speed the car breaks loose earlier, so a wet lap
pays more style than a dry one. Cutting top speed would only have made the
race longer.

Eased over ~2.5 s, not switched, because a shower that took hold between one
frame and the next would change the car's handling mid-corner. The ribbon's
own material wets and dries with it (read back from buildRoadMesh rather than
duplicating the finish presets, so it cannot drift out of step), and the HUD
names the cause and the number: a car that has quietly lost a fifth of its
cornering grip with nothing on screen is indistinguishable from a car that
has started handling badly, and the player will blame the game. The AI lifts
for corners on the same curve — a weather effect only the human felt would be
a handicap, not a condition.

THE PACK GETS THE SLIPSTREAM TOO. A rival could never reel in a car it was
following, so one that dropped two lengths back stayed there for the rest of
the race and the field never fought over anything. Rivals now tow off each
other and off the player. Gain is 0.09 against the player's 0.12, because the
AI holds a line and does not think to pull out, so it sits in a tow far more
of the time; the same number compounded into the pack circulating faster than
anyone driving it. Measured over a lap: mean rival tow 0.088, eight of nine
rivals in a meaningful tow at some point, field inside 156 m.

THE CROSSING. One telegraphed hazard per circuit — two boulders that sweep
across the road on a 9.5 s cycle behind a painted hazard band, two flashing
beacons and a HUD callout. Everything else on the track is static: you learn
where it is once and it is the same every lap. This is the one feature whose
answer changes each time you arrive, so the same corner is a different
problem on lap 1 and lap 3. Placed on a straight (on a bend the sweep line is
a chord across a curving road, so one end leaves the tarmac) and kept 120 m
clear of any drift zone.

Getting it right was mostly finding out where a boulder is allowed to be:

- Two, not one. One boulder on a 12.5 m ribbon always leaves nine metres of
  clear road, so there is nothing to do but notice it.
- The gap started at 4.5 m. Each boulder blocks ~2.8 m once the car's own
  width is counted, so that "gap" was negative — the pair was a wall. 7.5 m
  leaves a real slot; verified that the narrowest clear stretch at any point
  in the sweep is 1.9 m and never under 1.2, so there is always a way through.
- They only exist ON the road now, at road height. There is no good resting
  place beside the tarmac: the ground there is whatever the realm put down,
  and at Sunset Bay it is a ten-metre drop to the beach. Parked on the terrain
  a boulder sat in mid-air over the sea, and the slope was steep enough that
  15 cm of lateral slide moved it 1.1 m vertically — a visible hop every
  cycle. Parked on the road plane it hung in the sky. Nothing is lost: the
  telegraph was never the boulders, it is the band, the beacons and the
  callout. Collision is bounded to the same window, so an invisible boulder
  16 m out on the verge can no longer flatten a car running wide.
- The pair turns round the instant a sweep ENDS, not at the end of the cycle.
  `side` is the side the next sweep departs from and the idle position derives
  from it, so while it still said "left" for the five idle seconds after a
  left-to-right sweep, the boulders teleported 22 m back across the scenery.
  Measured as a 31 m single-frame jump; now the largest per-frame movement
  over 60 s is 0.171 m, exactly the sweep step.
- `placeSetPiece` positions the meshes itself. `update()` returns early while
  loading or counting down, so the boulders sat at the WORLD ORIGIN for the
  whole countdown and teleported 422 m to the crossing on the first racing

- The hit shoves you away from the boulder that got you. The first version set
  `spinRate`, which does nothing on the ground — it is only integrated while
  airborne, as the twist-ramp corkscrew. Verified the kick direction from both

Put the fork back, and fix the nine things that made it wrong

The alternate routes were torn out with the note "the open fork corridor let
the car wander off-road (OOB + sink) and the separate curve felt bad". That
diagnosis blamed the fork. The cause was that nothing outside `freeDrive` had
ever been told a second road existed.

`freeDrive` projects onto whichever road is nearer and walls you onto it, and
reports `lateral` relative to THAT road. Everything else in the game reads
`freeDrive.lateral` as "metres from the main centreline". So out on a branch
bowing 16 m away it reported ZERO, and every system silently believed the car
was on the racing line. Measured, parked on the branch centreline at the apex:
`freeDrive.lateral` 0.00 while `track.project` put the car 17.23 m off the
main road, with thirteen entities in the fork span sitting at laterals the
collision test would have matched. Taking the fork would have vacuumed up
every chip on the road you did not drive.

One `onMainRoad` guard now gates the nine systems that share that assumption:
entity pickups, the ramp ride-up (whose own guard used the rail-era `onBranch`
field and had quietly stopped guarding), drift zones, the crossing, near
misses, car-to-car contact, the lane bonus, and both halves of the slipstream.

And the rest of it:

- THE SINK. The car's height came from `track.pointAt(position, lateral)` —
  the main road — whichever road it was on. On a branch that is a different
  piece of geometry at a different elevation, so you floated where the fork
  was lower and were buried where it was higher. `surfaceY()` asks the road
  you are actually on; measured error on the branch is now 0.000 m.
- THE STEERING ASSIST STEERED YOU OFF IT. Pure pursuit to a point on the main
  centreline, always — so the moment you turned onto a fork it turned you
  back. Measured: 34 frames of 600 spent on the branch. It now aims down the
  branch, with a shorter look-ahead, because a 41 m look on a 140 m open path
  clamps to its final point near the exit and the car aims at a fixed spot
  instead of following the road.
- THE TREES. The scenery bands are laid out from the main centreline and reach
  40 m out, so rows 2 and 3 planted a forest down the middle of the alternate
  road. The branch centrelines now go into the same sample set that every
  "is this spot clear of the circuit" test already used, so one change covers
  every call site; `obstacleClear` refuses branch positions too. 0 of 2,636
  obstacles now land on a branch.
- THE ISLAND WAS IN BOTH ROADS. Sized from `bulge`, it came out a 6.6 m cone in
  a 4.6 m median: it overlapped the main road at 5.5 m (drivable to 6.6) and
  the branch at 12.1 m (inner edge 11.2). It is now measured from where the
  branch's inner edge actually falls.
- THE BRANCH WAS NARROWER THAN THE ROAD. Built at 5 m half-width against the
  main road's 6.25, while the containment walls are absolute at 5.6/6.6 — so
  the fork could be driven a metre and a half past its own tarmac. The car
  spent 47% of the branch flagged off-road, grinding a wall out over nothing.
  Same width now; off-road fell to 18.6%, and the lateral profile shows that
  is entirely the last 10%, where the two ribbons overlap at the merge — the
  body of the branch peaks at 4.3 m.
- THE SIGN WAS IN THE ROAD. It is built as a gantry with two narrow central
  posts, and it was placed on the centreline at the mouth, so the posts stood
  on the racing line — not registered as solid, so you drove through a steel
  sign at 115 mph. Now on the verge 34 m upstream, which is also where a
  direction sign is any use.
- IT WAS ALWAYS THE SLOWER ROAD. The side was picked from a character code,
  which on a straight makes the branch a lens, and a lens is always longer
  than its chord: 154 m on a 130 m span, half a second of pure penalty. The
  fork now slides along the lap to the bendiest span available and bows to the
  measured INSIDE of it, and the construction's tangent leads and taper are
  tightened. Forest: 138 m (8 m penalty, was 24). Void Circuit: 119 m — a
  genuine shortcut.
- AND WHEN IT IS STILL SLOWER, IT PAYS. A fork cannot pay in pickups: entities
  live in main-track (distance, lateral) space, and on a branch that second
  coordinate means something else, so "a boost pad on the fork" is not
  expressible without re-addressing every entity in the game. It pays in style
  instead — see the whole branch through and it is a chain link. Bail back onto
  the main road half way and it pays nothing.

Verified on two realms: 4.4 s held on the fork covering 87% of it, 0 gems
collected while on it, no respawn, and all four of this session's gimmicks
(drift zones, pad chains, the crossing, the fork) coexisting on one circuit.

Known and left: a ghost lap recorded via the fork replays at a branch-relative
lateral on the main road, so the ghost cuts that corner. It is a translucent
pace reference, not a physical car, and the alternative is a gap in the
recording.

line of text through it every few seconds.

DRIFT ZONES ARE GONE, REPLACED BY APEXES. The zones worked. The corner finder
was sound, the gauge filled, the chain paid — and they were still wrong,
because four 130 m bands of violet chevrons covered a tenth of the circuit.
On a game whose pitch is how it looks, a scoring hook should not be the thing
hiding the view. They were also the third mechanic paying for the same input:
the drift boost pays for sliding, the style chain pays for sliding, and then a
painted corner paid for sliding again.

An apex is a POINT, so marking it takes two red-and-white kerb blocks on the
inside of the bend and no paint at all. Clip it at speed, on the tarmac, and
it pays into the chain. The corner-finding code is unchanged — it was always
the good half — but it now locates the tightest point of each corner rather
than its span, which matters more than expected: two of the four corners on
the measured circuit are tightest on ENTRY, so their apex is early, and
marking the midpoint would have pointed at the wrong piece of road.

hands-off lap clips ZERO apexes, because the steering assist holds the
centreline. A drift zone could be partly satisfied by the car driving itself.

Give the car a friction circle, so corners finally cost something

The audit's one open finding was that the game has exactly one speed: over a
full lap, mean 122.9 mph against a maximum of 123, standard deviation 1.9,
100% of the lap within 5 mph of top. Top speed arrived 3.3 s after the lights
and never left. With no speed to lose there is none to regain, so the arcade
loop — lift, commit to a line, get it back on the exit — had no first step,
and every gimmick added on top of it was decoration on a constant-velocity
drive.

Two changes, and the second is the one that mattered.

CORNERING SCRUB. A corner is the car turning, and turning is lateral
acceleration: yaw rate × speed. Above what the tyres hold, the excess comes
out of forward speed. Measured from the ACTUAL heading change rather than from
player input, because the steering assist turns the car too — if only your own
steering scrubbed, the assist would keep carrying you through every corner at
full speed, which is the bug being fixed.

Tuned against the lap's own distribution rather than from physics. The car's
lateral acceleration runs p50 4.1, p80 6.3, p95 9.7, peak 20.4 m/s². My first
guess of 12 (~1.2g, which sounds right for a car) put 1.4% of the lap over the
limit and changed nothing. At 5, a quarter of the lap is over it.

THE FRICTION CIRCLE, which is what actually worked. The scrub alone could not
win: acceleration is ~12.5 m/s² and a typical corner's scrub is ~7, so the
engine simply powered through every bend — 82% of the lap still sat in one
10 mph band even after the scrub rate was raised five-fold. Raising it further
would have been a number fight. A tyre has ONE budget of grip and cornering
spends it; what is left is what you can put down as drive. Taking the grip
away from the engine is the thing that is actually happening, and it produces
the loop directly: turn in, lose the ability to accelerate, bleed down to the
speed the corner allows, get it all back on the exit.

Measured over a lap, before → after:

  standard deviation      1.9  →  13.5 mph
  speed range          121-123 →  69-126
  time in one 10 mph band 100% →  66%
  corners (70-90 mph)       0% →  18%
  off-road                  0% →  0%     (the assist still holds the line)

Hands-off the player still finishes first by 3.1 km, so the AI has not been
handed the race — rivals already lift for corners via `cornerLift`, now
scaled by the same grip stat.

The grip limit is multiplied by the kart's grip stat and by the weather, so
both finally mean what they say: a better-handling kart carries more speed
through a bend, and a wet road takes it away.

Let alternate routes hold things, and put a ramp on one

ENTITIES NOW KNOW WHICH ROAD THEY ARE ON. This was the structural reason the
first fork had to be deleted: an entity's lateral is "metres from a
centreline" and nothing recorded WHICH centreline, so every pickup, pad and
ramp in the game belonged to the main road by construction. A branch could
never hold anything, which is why it could never be worth taking.

`Entity.road` and `ramps[].road` are -1 for the main circuit or an index into
`branches`. A branch entity is placed along that branch's own curve, stores
its `dist` as the main-track distance the branch maps to — so the distance
buckets and every lap check keep working untouched — and only collides while
you are on that road. The blanket `if (!this.onMainRoad) return` in collide()
is gone, replaced by a per-entity check.

THE ROUTE NOW CARRIES A BOOST CHAIN INTO A RAMP. The ramp is the point:
cornering load is the rate the direction of travel turns, times speed, and in
the air both are irrelevant — so a jump carries speed through a bend that
would otherwise scrub half of it away. That is only true because the friction
circle made corners cost something in the first place; it is also why the
route bows to the OUTSIDE now, where the wider radius is worth more than the
metres it costs. The opposite was true when corners were free.

Measured on the fork at Enchanted Forest, identical start and finish:

  main line   6.05 s, exits at 44 mph, no air
  route       7.45 s, exits at 86 mph, 1.47 s airborne, 4 m up, 2.5 s of boost

So it is spectacular and still SLOWER — about a second, closing to 0.85 s when
measured 300 m past the merge but never winning. The cost is the peel-off: a
16 m lateral move in ~25 m of road is a hard turn, and hard turns now cost
speed. Honest state of it, written down rather than claimed otherwise.

Proof the road separation works: boost fired for 2.48 s on the route and 0.00 s
on the main line, so branch pickups do not leak to the road beside them.

simulation.

Give every realm its own ground, from the same photograph

Ten of the seventeen realms borrowed another realm's ground albedo and
recoloured it with `color: groundTint`. That is a MULTIPLY: it can only
darken, and it cannot move a hue. The code already knew — there is a comment
explaining that the coast road could not use the forest albedo because
"forest tinted straw stays GREEN" — so snow, sand, red desert, a dusty
waterfront and a night city were all the same pale rock with the brightness
turned down.

`recolourAlbedo` maps the source photo's LUMINANCE through the realm's own
dark → base → speck ramp. Those colours already existed on every realm: they
were written for the procedural fallback and never used on the PBR path.
Grain, cracks and variation all survive because they live in the luminance;
the colour is replaced outright, so snow can be white with cool shadows and
the desert can be genuinely red. The source's own luminance range is measured
and stretched first — a rock photo occupies maybe a quarter of the range, and
feeding that straight into a ramp uses only the middle of it.

No new files, so nothing lands on the texture budget; one canvas pass per
race at load.

Measured, all from the same photograph:

  Hokkai Pass  palette #eef4fb snow      → cool blue-white, shadows #677a95
  Mirage Mile  palette #d9b47e sand      → #e0be88
  Basin Run    palette #b5673f red rock  → #9f5a38

A bug worth writing down, because it will happen again: `new
THREE.Color(0xd9b47e)` does NOT store 0xd9b47e. With colour management on the
constructor converts that sRGB hex into the linear working space, so
`.r/.g/.b` come out around 0.71/0.46/0.22 instead of 0.85/0.71/0.49 — and
writing them into an 8-bit canvas treats linear values as sRGB ones, which
darkens and over-saturates. Mirage asked for #d9b47e and rendered #bf8540. I
misdiagnosed it as the photo's luminance distribution and added a gamma to
recentre the ramp, which pushed it to #af7637 — further away. The actual fix
is one call: `getHex(THREE.SRGBColorSpace)`, asking for the number back in the
space it was written in.

Two things I had recommended in the same breath turned out to be already
done, and done well — I should have read before advising. Car paint is a
MeshPhysicalMaterial with clearcoat 0.95 against a genuine HDR float
environment probe with a ~30x sun, and `paintByHeight` already bakes
contact-AO gradients into the instanced scenery's vertex colours. Neither
needed touching.

Give the sand ripples, the snow drifts and the desert cracks

The recolour fixed hue; it could not fix structure. Ten realms shared one
rock photograph, so after recolouring, the Gulf highway and the snowbound
pass still had the same cracks in the same places.

`groundDetailField` synthesises the three ground surfaces that are regular
enough for synthesis to beat a photograph: wind ripples are periodic, drifts
are low-frequency and smooth, and dried mud is a cell structure (distance to
the second-nearest of a jittered point set). It blends into the luminance the
colour ramp reads — 55% photo, 45% pattern — so the photograph's grain still
does the work that stops any of this looking like a gradient.

IT GOES IN THE ALBEDO, NOT A NORMAL MAP. I wrote a normal-map generator
first, wired it in, and measured the ground having no normal map at all. The
engine does `groundMat.normalMap = null` one line after taking makeGround's
material, with the reason attached: "terrain fills the screen — drop the
per-pixel normal cost". So the generated map was built and thrown away. That
is a deliberate optimisation and the right one; baking the pattern into the
albedo's luminance costs nothing per frame, survives it, and still reads as
structure because it is the light and shade a structure would produce.

Buying photographs was the alternative and does not fit: normal maps are the
expensive half of a texture set here (111-161 kB against 9-78 kB for the
albedos) and one more set would spend the entire remaining 262 kB of budget
on a single realm.

Ripples run at 9 cycles per tile, not 34. The ground tiles at 220 over a
2,800 m disc, so a tile is ~12.7 m — 34 cycles is a 37 cm wavelength, which is
what a real wind ripple measures and is completely invisible from a car fifty
metres away. 9 gives ~1.4 m corrugations that actually read while driving.
Verified by counting mean-crossings in the built texture: 9 cycles, 1.41 m.

Assigned: sand to Mirage Mile, Sunset Bay and the dunes; snow to Hokkai Pass
and Crystal Peaks; dried mud to Basin Run. Realms whose ground really is rock
or grass keep the photograph's own grain.

Cost, measured: 1.6 ms for sand, 28 ms for dried mud, once per race. No new
files, so the texture budget is untouched at 1338/1600 kB.
