Halve the cars' draw calls, and spend it on making them round

Asked to improve how the cars look, I measured them first. The numbers were
the opposite way round from the assumption:

  frame draw calls   1,232
  ten cars             798 meshes — 65% of the frame's entire draw-call budget
  ten cars          42,092 triangles — 0.5% of the frame's triangles
  per car               80 meshes, 4,209 triangles

On a renderer that is draw-call bound, the cars were spending the budget on
the wrong axis. And 64 of each car's 76 meshes were WHEELS: `mergeStaticParts`
skips anything tagged `userData.wheel` — correctly, because a wheel rotates
relative to the body. But every part of ONE wheel rotates together, so a wheel
can be merged internally for exactly the reason it cannot be merged
externally. `mergeByMaterial(group, false)` does that; 16 meshes per wheel
become 6.

That paid for the detail, because tessellation is free here and draw calls are
not. Tyre 16 sides → 32 (a 16-gon is a visible decagon from a chase camera
three metres behind it), rim barrel 8 → 24, lip torus 4x18 → 8x28, hub
12 → 20, brake disc 16 → 28.

And the body. A rib gives six points per half, so however smoothly the spine
is splined lengthwise, every section around the car is a ten-sided tube — the
roof was one flat quad from the deck edge to the centre line, which is why
roofs read as folded card. `refineSection` subdivides the cross-section and
blends the spline OUT wherever the section turns hard, so the sill and the
shoulder crease stay exactly where the rib table put them. Those edges are the
design — the existing comments say so directly, "resampling six times splines
the edges out of existence" — and rounding them off would have been a
regression dressed as an improvement.

  frame draw calls      975  (-257)
  per car                40 meshes (-50%), 7,745 triangles (x1.8)
  wheel meshes per car   64 → 24

Verified across all nine grid cars: every model builds, no NaN vertices,
7,420-7,788 triangles each.

One bug on the way. `refineSection` first inserted a VARIABLE number of points
per segment, skipping insertion entirely on sharp corners — so different ribs
came out different lengths, and the loft skins rib i to rib i+1 point by point
with its own doc stating every rib must have the same count. The engine died
indexing past the end of a shorter rib. It now always inserts the same number
and lets the blend decide where they sit; where the blend is zero they land on
the straight edge, so an edge stays an edge and only the vertex count changes.

Honest about the result: the visual gain is clear up close and modest at chase
distance. The draw-call saving is the larger win — a third of the budget
handed back, on the axis that actually binds.

Grade the frame toward the illustration look it was already aiming at

Shown six pieces of JDM anime / vapourwave car art as a target. Reading the
engine first this time: the game is already pointed that way. Eight realms run
`posterSun`, which flat-shades the terrain and gives the car paint an emissive
livery so bodies read as blocks of colour rather than gradients, and lofted car
shells already carry a toon ink outline. The geometry side of the reference
look is built.

What the references have that a PBR frame does not is two things, and both are
in the lighting and the palette rather than the models: light falls in HARD
BANDS instead of a smooth ramp, and the whole image sits in one hue family
with only the neon escaping it.

Both are now terms in FilmGradeShader — a pass already in the chain, so there
is no new render target and no new pass:

- CEL banding quantises LUMINANCE, not colour. Posterising rgb independently
  shifts hues at every step and turns a sunset into confetti; scaling the
  colour by the ratio of banded to actual luminance keeps the hue exactly and
  steps only the brightness, which is what cel shading is. The step is
  softened by `fwidth` so it is a painted edge rather than an aliased one.
- DUOTONE pulls the frame toward one hue ramp, but ONLY where it is
  unsaturated. In the reference art the world sits in a single colour family
  and the neon is the one thing that escapes — tinting everything equally
  would kill exactly the accents that make the look work. Verified on Neon
  Metro: the cyan and magenta kerbs stay vivid through it.

Strength is per realm and comes from the realm's own palette, so each world is
graded toward itself rather than through one global filter. Poster realms take
it further (cel 0.55 / duo 0.34) than the rest (0.22 / 0.14), because that is
already their declared intent.

Cost: none measurable. Rendering a frame takes 7-9 ms with the terms on, off,
or with the whole grade pass disabled — they are a few ALU ops in a pass that
already runs. No GL errors; the derivatives use is WebGL2 core.

Checked for a regression on the way: poster mode sets `flatShading = true` on
car paint, so the subdivision work in the last two commits could have made
those realms MUSHIER by shrinking the facets. It has not — the car still
reads as a bold colour block on Sunset Hills.

Known and not fixed: the checkered start line moirés badly at grazing angles,
and the banding sharpens it. That aliasing predates this change; the grade
makes it more visible.

Push the illustration grade to where you can actually see it

You said you could not see the last change on the deployed build. It was
deployed — 46183df went to production and succeeded — so the problem was the
change itself, not the pipeline. Measured on Sunset Hills, the shipped grade
moved the frame by a few percent: five bands can only ever shift a pixel by
half a band, so the biggest possible step was around 10% brightness, and it
was mixed in at 0.55. That is a change you have to be told about to notice.

Four things, in the same pass as before — still no new render target:

1. FOUR bands, not five, and the steps are now pushed apart around a pivot
   near this game's typical luminance. Quantising alone keeps the average and
   just rounds it, so the bands sit on top of each other; the spread is what
   gives the hard terminator the reference art is built on.

2. The banding now reads LOW-FREQUENCY luminance — a five-tap cross rather
   than the pixel itself. Quantising the raw value let gravel speckle and
   grass noise wander across band edges, which came out as blotches. Averaging
   first puts the steps where the LIGHT changes and lets texture ride on top
   of them. I had assumed the opposite problem first (that the anti-aliasing
   term was eating the effect) and measured before acting: only 6% of the
   frame was fully softened, median gradient 0.0118, so 88% of the banding was
   already applying. That hypothesis was wrong.

3. The duotone is now luminance-preserving. The old ramp multiplied by
   (0.35 + l*0.9) and quietly ate a fifth of the frame's brightness; pushed
   to a bolder setting it took 37%. Renormalising the ramp to the pixel's own
   luminance makes it a pure recolour. Net effect: the new grade is BOLDER and
   BRIGHTER than the one it replaces — frame mean 0.2124 against the shipped
   0.1936, on an ungraded 0.2485.

4. Halftone: a 45-degree print dot screen in the shadows only, the dot growing
   with ink coverage as it does in print. Pitch is in device pixels and scales
   with dpr, so it is the same size to the eye on a retina panel as on a 1x.
   This is the last element of the six references not previously built.

Per realm: poster realms 0.9 / 0.5 / 0.5, the rest 0.55 / 0.28 / 0.28.

Checked the thing most likely to break: Neon Metro, where a blue duotone over
a neon realm should be worst. It is not — kerb saturation 0.715 -> 0.705,
windows 0.768 -> 0.740, sky unchanged. The neon escapes the tint as intended.
I also thought the fixed pivot would crush dark realms and was ready to build
an adaptive one; sweeping the pivot from 0.34 to 0.06 on Metro moved frame
exposure by 7 points total (-14% to -7%), so the fixed value stays.

Cost: the whole pass is 0.2-0.8 ms at 2.76 MP by GPU timer query, and the bold
version does not separate from the shipped one inside that spread. Note that
wall-clock timing around composer.render() cannot resolve this at all — the
spread within one configuration was 5.23 ms and "pass disabled" measured
SLOWER than "pass enabled", which is how you know the harness is noise. The
earlier "7-9 ms, no measurable cost" reading was that same unusable harness.

Verified on three realms covering both code paths and both exposure extremes:
Sunset Hills (warm poster), Neon Metro (dark non-poster), Hokkai Pass (bright
poster — snow stays clean, the halftone correctly stays out of the highlights).
typecheck, lint, build and all three test suites pass.

Two things to know. The halftone is screen-space by construction, so it does
not track the world — that is how print halftone works, but it is the first
thing to turn down if it reads as a static overlay in motion. And the checkered
start line still moirés at grazing angles; that aliasing predates this and the
harder banding keeps making it more visible.

Fix the sky, reach the alternate routes, and give the speed somewhere to go

Five things you reported, all measured before and after.

SKY. The black disc at the zenith and the hard seam across the upper sky were
mine, from the bolder grade. Two causes. Band zero sits at zero, the spread
pushes it negative, it clamps, and the pixel is multiplied by nothing — so the
darkest part of a smooth sky became a hole with a razor edge. And the dome
already carries its own 26-band posterisation, authored in equirect space, so
a second screen-space quantisation on top of it beat against the first.

So: no band may land on zero, the multiplier is bounded to 0.6-1.6 (typical
mid-frame ratios measured 0.77-1.18, so it only binds at the tails), and the
cel term is masked off the sky entirely. The mask rides in the ALPHA channel —
the dome and its cloud deck write zero, everything else writes one, and the
pass chain carries it through untouched. Measured: sky luminance now changes
0.00% between cel on and off while the ground still changes 4.71%.

Depth was the textbook way to do that and is a dead end here, which cost most
of the time on this: EffectComposer ping-pongs between two targets with an odd
number of swaps per frame, so which one the scene lands in alternates, and a
DepthTexture shared by both sampled as zero everywhere. Two more traps on the
way: an alpha set before the tone-map and colour-space includes does not
survive them, and onBeforeCompile edits are silently dropped unless the
material also carries its own customProgramCacheKey — programs are cached on
parameters, and the hook is not one of them.

ALT ROUTES. Three separate faults.

The fork was inside a cave. REALM_SPLITS places each fork clear of that
realm's tunnels and rivers, and then the bend-seeking search sild it up to
600 m downstream without checking what it was sliding into. On Enchanted
Forest the fork is authored at 244 m to miss the cave at 756-838; the search
moved it to 819 and put the mouth 19 m inside the rock. Candidates that touch
a tunnel or a river crossing are now rejected. Forest 344-474, Crystal Peaks
1620-1740, both 0 m inside anything.

It was also unreachable on its own terms. Which road you are on is decided by
the nearer centreline, and the wall holds you 6.6 m from it — but the branch
bows 16 m out, so crossing needs more than 8 m and the wall will not allow it.
The window was 24 m of road, half a second, and inside it the car had to be
already pinned against the wall. Measured: holding steer into the fork put the
car on the branch for 8 frames out of 360, which is only the shared point at
the mouth. Now, while the two ribbons still overlap, the wall on that side
opens far enough to reach the crossover. A quarter-second flick of the wheel
gives 3.3 s on the branch; steering nothing at all still gives 0.03 s, so it
never happens by accident.

And it is on the minimap now, dashed and in the fork sign's amber.

SPEED. The dial stopped at 150 and a measured lap sat between 57 and 123 with
a median of 89 — most of a race in the bottom half of a dial that never
reached its own ceiling. Worse, the car was at the drive floor for 48% of the
lap: CORNER_GRIP was set to 5 on the reasoning that a quarter of the lap over
the limit would make corners cost something, and it was never checked
afterwards. It was not a quarter. More than half the race ran with four
fifths of the engine taken away, which is what "the acceleration is weird"
was.

MAX_SPEED 46 -> 56 (corner speed is sqrt(grip x radius) and does not depend on
it, so this widens the gap between slowest corner and fastest straight rather
than scaling everything), CORNER_GRIP 5 -> 11, dial 240. 15 was too far the
other way — the car sat at 96% of top speed and corners went free again. At 11
the lap reads 117 through the slow corners, median 176, 222 flat out, leaving
the top of the dial for nitro and a tow. Lap time 64.5 s -> 47.1 s, still 0%
off-road.

WATERFALLS. The landmark placer searches for LEVEL ground, which is right for
a castle and exactly wrong for water: Enchanted Forest had a rock slab with a
sheet of water down its face standing upright in an open meadow, no cliff, no
watercourse, no pool. It was the flattest spot available, which is precisely
why it looked absurd. Cliff-seeking props now invert the test and search along
the lap as well as out from it — sampling the realm on a grid, 6.6% of spots
clear a 14 m drop across the footprint, so they exist, they were just never
where the three nominal distances pointed. If nothing near is steep enough,
nothing is placed. Forest went from one in a field to two on ground dropping
14.8 m and 15.0 m; Crystal Peaks puts one on a 25 m face.

typecheck, lint, build and all three suites pass.

Not fixed, and worth knowing: resetting the car to distance 0 from the debug

ground and cannot say whether it can happen in play.

term topped out near 0.108 — an 11% lift in the tightest hairpin, against its

two. And because `cornerSkill` varies 0.82-1.20 per racer, corners are now
where the field separates, which is what a grid of drivers should look like.

Fix the size budget, add a car-catalogue tripwire, and notice CI was red

CI HAS BEEN FAILING FOR SEVEN COMMITS and I did not look. The Next 16 upgrade
removed `.next/app-build-manifest.json`; `test/budgets.mjs` reads it, so it has
crashed on a missing file since 8131af3. It runs in CI after the build and is
deliberately NOT part of `npm test` — which is exactly how it hid, because
`npm test` kept coming back green locally and I trusted that instead of the
workflow. Every commit since the upgrade is red on that one step.

The test was also measuring the wrong thing, which is the more interesting
half. It summed `app-build-manifest.json`'s chunk set for /page and /layout,
reported ~195 kB and passed happily, while the emitted HTML referenced the
three.js chunk as an async <script> the browser fetched on first paint. The
manifest and the document disagreed and the document is what the browser
obeys — the same lesson as yesterday's `rootMainFiles` confusion, arrived at
from the other direction.

Let you watch the lap you just drove

WATCH LAP on the results screen rebuilds the world and plays the last
complete lap back. The recording is four numbers a physics step — the two
ground coordinates, the heading and the jump height — because everything
else the frame needs (wheel spin, body pitch, the whole camera) is
DERIVED from those, so it comes out the same on the way back. A 60-second
lap is about 3,100 samples.

Two buffers, not one: the current lap fills as it is driven and moves to
the "last" slot at the line, so what gets offered is a lap that was
completed rather than however much of one you were partway through.

The recording rides home on GameResult rather than being pulled off the
engine through a ref, because the engine is torn down the moment the race
ends — by the time React has a results screen to put a button on there is
nothing left to ask. saveScore and submitGlobalScore both pick their
fields explicitly, so it never reaches storage or the network, and the
button is only offered when a lap actually exists.

During playback update() hands over to replayStep completely. Driving the
physics from recorded positions would fight the recording, and the rivals
have no business racing a lap that is already over — so they are hidden
rather than left parked on the grid where they would otherwise stand for
the whole minute. The HUD drops the half of itself that is a control
surface (the nitro cells advertise a key that does nothing, the footer
offered a pause for a finished race) and the score panel carries the lap
clock instead. Escape leaves.

playback reaching 220 mph with the clock and minimap tracking it, zero
rivals drawn, the wrap at the last sample looping to 0 with the camera
snapped rather than panning a lap backwards, and Escape returning to a
results screen that still offers the lap again.

Carry a signed-in player's progress between devices

AUDIT item 21. POST /api/profile, keyed by the Google subject id, holding
settings, career and any season in progress.

THE MERGE IS THE FEATURE. Whole-document last-write-wins is the obvious
implementation and it silently destroys progress: drive three races on a
laptop, then two on a phone that has not synced since this morning, and
one of those sessions is gone with nothing anywhere saying so. Career
counters are monotonic — races, podiums, wins, metres, best score only
ever go up — so they merge element-wise by maximum and neither device can
subtract. Preferences and a part-raced season are not monotonic and have
no sensible element-wise merge, so those take the newer document whole,
including a newer null season: that is one the player FINISHED, and
resurrecting it on the other machine would be a bug, not a rescue.

That logic lives in profileMerge.ts, importing only types, so it can be
tested in plain Node without dragging localStorage and fetch along.
npm run test:sync is in CI and was proven against three injected
regressions — last-write-wins on a counter, the one-time seeding flag
taken from the newer side, and a field-by-field season merge. The first
of those is caught only by the 72-pair invariant sweep, not by any named
case, which is why the sweep is there.

IT IS AUTHENTICATED. This is the third write endpoint in the project and
the first two shipped wide open (B4/B5). Subject ids are not secret, so
an unauthenticated profile route would let anyone who learned one read
and overwrite that person's career. Every call verifies the credential
through Google's own tokeninfo and checks aud against our client id —
without that last check a token minted for any other Google app would be
accepted, with a perfectly real signature and issuer. The credential is
held in memory for the session only: it is a bearer token for this route
and expires in an hour, so persisting it would buy nothing.

Verified against a stub KV with the route configured: a forged token
carrying the correct aud in its own payload is rejected 401 and the store
is never touched (the only traffic is the rate limiter); push and pull
round-trip; two subjects cannot see each other's profile; an oversize
body is refused 413. Unconfigured, which is how this deployment stands,
it answers {synced:false, reason} and the game runs entirely from local
storage — verified, along with both home-screen states. NOT verified: a
real Google credential, which cannot be minted without a client id. The
happy path was exercised with verification temporarily stubbed, which
does not prove the tokeninfo call itself.

Stop the cars shaking at speed on high-refresh screens

The simulation steps at a fixed 60 Hz and the latest step was rendered
as-is. On a 120 Hz display every other frame showed a car that had not
moved while the chase camera kept easing toward it, so the car lurched
forward and back every frame, more the faster it went. Rivals the same.

Now the player's pose and the rivals are drawn between the last two
steps, and the true state is restored as soon as the frame is drawn.
The camera's per-frame easing is converted to real time, so it settles
the same at any refresh rate.

player 5.21 -> 0.04 px at 120 Hz, 4.71 -> 0.04 px at 144 Hz;

Add the campaign's rules: events, goals, the star judge, and sync

THE DUSK LINE: twelve events in three chapters ordered by the hour in each
world's sky — golden hour, sunset, night — and a finale on the Neon Run
highway. Three goals an event, judged from the GameResult the race already
produces: finishing position, a share of the gems on offer, tricks, clean
lanes, and for the finale distance and time. No per-track lap times or
scores, because nobody has measured those per world.

The engine gets two opt-in fields and nothing else: targetDistanceM ends
a Neon Run (it otherwise only ends on quit, which reports nothing), and
gemsOffered says how many gems the race put down, so a gem goal is the
same difficulty on a 2.4 km lap and a 6.5 km one. The finish sequence is
one method now, shared by the last lap and the distance.

Stars are a per-event bitmask that only grows; they sync through the
profile by bitwise OR, so a stale device cannot take one away.
test:campaign checks every event's realm and goals, that each chapter can
be opened by the stars before it, and the judge; it runs in CI.

+# Analysis plan for the confirmatory run
+
+Status: written after exploring the Upworthy exploratory release, before the confirmatory release has been
+opened. Nothing in this repository has read, counted or hashed the confirmatory file. (When it was
+downloaded, its sha256 and raw line count were printed to confirm the download; no rows were parsed.) Once this plan and
+the code are committed, `ANALYSIS_PLAN.lock` is created and the confirmatory analysis is run once:
+
+```
+shasum -a 256 ANALYSIS_PLAN.md > ANALYSIS_PLAN.lock
+uv run forensics run --release confirmatory
+```
+
+The code refuses to load the confirmatory file unless `ANALYSIS_PLAN.lock` exists. If the lock contains a
+sha256 digest, it must match this file. The results go to `reports/confirmatory.md` and
+`reports/results_confirmatory.json`, and are reported whatever they show.
+
+## Data
+
+- File: `data/raw/upworthy-archive-confirmatory-packages-03.12.2020.csv`, expected sha256
+  `b2a88288c88f2b67d40413c9bdbebe79a1c0b5d9a9354180549f59f3bfff685f` (checked by `scripts/fetch_data.sh`).
+- Read with `pandas.read_csv` (fields contain embedded newlines and HTML). One row per package (arm); arms
+  are grouped by `clickability_test_id`. `created_at` is parsed as a naive timestamp (the archive says its
+  timezone is unknown).
+- Pipeline check: count packages and tests and compare with the paper's 105,551 packages within 22,743
+  tests. A mismatch is reported, and the analysis still runs.
+
+## Exclusion (Matias et al. 2024 correction)
+
+- A test is excluded when its first package (earliest `created_at`) was created on or after
+  2013-06-25 00:00:00 and before 2014-01-11 00:00:00, i.e. "from June 25, 2013 through the end of
+  January 10, 2014".
+- Reported alongside: counts under the any-package and all-packages rules, and with both window edges
+  shifted by -24, -12, +12 and +24 hours.
+- Sample-ratio check: per multi-arm test, chi-square test of equal impressions across arms; share with
+  p < 0.001 inside and outside the window.
+
+## Definitions
+
+- Arms with fewer than 100 impressions are dropped before anything else.
+- Reference arm: the arm in a test with the earliest `created_at` (ties broken by file row order).
+- Comparison: every other arm vs the reference. Difference `d = p_arm - p_ref`; relative difference
+  `d / p_ref` (undefined when `p_ref = 0`). Standard error from the pooled rate,
+  `s = sqrt(p_pool (1 - p_pool) (1/n_arm + 1/n_ref))`; comparisons with `s = 0` are dropped. Two-sided
+  pooled two-proportion z-test.
+- Identical-arm pairs: within a kept test, arms with identical `headline`, `eyecatcher_id` and `excerpt`
+  (missing values treated as empty strings); the first two such arms by creation time form one pair.
+  Reported: number of pairs, share with p < 0.05, binomial test of that share against 5%, mean z squared
+  (phi).
+
+## Analysis 1: effect sizes and power
+
+- Quantiles (5, 25, 50, 75, 95) of `d` and of the relative difference; median |d|, median |relative d|,
+  share of comparisons with p < 0.05.
+- Per test: average arm size `n` (total impressions over arms) and pooled click rate `p`. MDE at 80% power,
+  two-sided alpha 0.05: `(z_0.975 + z_0.80) sqrt(2 p (1 - p) / n)`; relative MDE = MDE / p.
+- Typical true effect: median |theta| under the grid prior of analysis 3. Reported: share of tests with
+  MDE <= typical true effect, share with MDE <= median observed |d|, mean and median power at the typical
+  true effect.
+
+## Analysis 2: peeking
+
+- 20,000 simulated A/A tests. Each draws a kept test uniformly with replacement and uses its pooled rate
+  for both arms and its average arm size (rounded) for each arm. Impressions arrive in 100 equal batches
+  (batch edges `floor(n k / 100)`), with binomial clicks per batch.
+- Looks K in {1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100}: check after every 100/K batches. Naive: pooled z-test, reject at
+  the first |z| > 1.96. mSPRT: normal-mixture likelihood ratio of Johari et al. with pooled-variance
+  plug-in, mixing SD tau = 0.0036 (0.36 pp, the exploratory normal prior SD rounded, frozen), reject at the
+  first look with ratio >= 20.
+- Power: the same with a relative lift of 10%, 25% and 50% in the second arm; reported for a single final
+  z-test and for mSPRT with 10 and 100 looks.
+- Seeds: `numpy.random.default_rng([20261018, 1])` for A/A, `default_rng([20261018, 2, i])` for the i-th
+  lift.
+
+## Analysis 3: winner's curse
+
+- Priors are fit to all comparisons (`d`, `s`): normal prior N(mu, tau^2) by maximum marginal likelihood
+  (Nelder-Mead), and a grid NPMLE with 301 equally spaced points from min(d) to max(d), plus 0, fit by EM
+  (up to 3,000 iterations, stopping when the log-likelihood gain is below 1e-8 of its size).
+- Winner per test: the non-reference arm with the highest observed rate, kept if `d > 0`. Significant
+  winner: two-sided p < 0.05.
+- Reported: number of significant winners and share of tests; median observed lift; median shrinkage
+  `1 - posterior mean / d` under each prior; median posterior lift; share of significant winners with grid
+  posterior P(theta > 0) >= 0.95.
+- Sensitivity: multiply every `s` by sqrt(phi) from the identical-arm pairs (when phi > 1), refit the grid
+  prior, and report median shrinkage and the share of significant winners still clearing
+  |z| / sqrt(phi) > 1.96.
+- Examples: the significant winner with the largest shrinkage in percentage points, and the one whose
+  shrinkage is closest to the median.
+

+# Confirmatory results
+
+This is the single pre-registered run on the Upworthy confirmatory release, using the definitions, exclusions, seeds and criteria in `ANALYSIS_PLAN.md`. Every number is written by `uv run forensics run --release confirmatory`.
+
+## Exploratory vs confirmatory
+
+| Metric | Exploratory | Confirmatory | Criterion | Met |
+|---|---|---|---|---|
+| Share of tests in the correction window | 21.5% | 21.6% | within 2 pp of 21.6% | yes |
+| SRM p<0.001, inside window | 70.0% | 70.1% | > 25% | yes |
+| SRM p<0.001, outside window | 0.5% | 0.5% | < 2% | yes |
+| Identical-arm pairs with p<0.05 | 13.3% | 12.9% | > 5% | yes |
+| Identical-arm pairs, binomial test vs 5% | 6.9e-12 | 1.3e-42 | p < 0.01 | yes |
+| Median |difference| (pp) | 0.271 | 0.281 | descriptive |  |
+| Median |relative difference| | 24.5% | 24.8% | descriptive |  |
+| Normal prior SD (pp) | 0.362 | 0.380 | descriptive |  |
+| Typical true |effect|, grid (pp) | 0.148 | 0.189 | descriptive |  |
+| Median relative MDE | 64.1% | 63.4% | descriptive |  |
+| Tests powered for the typical effect | 0.03% | 0.08% | < 5% | yes |
+| Mean power at the typical effect | 10.3% | 13.3% | < 20% | yes |
+| A/A false positives, 1 look | 5.2% | 4.9% | within 1 pp of 5% | yes |
+| A/A false positives, 10 looks | 18.9% | 18.7% | >= 10% | yes |
+| A/A false positives, 100 looks | 30.4% | 30.6% | >= 20% | yes |
+| mSPRT false positives, 100 looks | 0.32% | 0.31% | <= 5.5% | yes |
+| Significant winners (share of tests) | 22.2% | 21.4% | descriptive |  |
+| Median shrinkage, grid prior | 40.5% | 40.6% | within 10 pp of exploratory | yes |
+| Median shrinkage, normal prior | 41.8% | 39.7% | within 10 pp of exploratory | yes |
+| Winners with P(true lift > 0) >= 95% | 42.1% | 38.3% | descriptive |  |
+| Median shrinkage, grid prior, inflated SEs | 83.3% | 88.3% | descriptive |  |
+
+## Upworthy pipeline checks
+
+The confirmatory file has 105,551 packages in 22,743 tests. The archive paper reports 105,551 packages within 22,743 tests for this release, so the counts match. Clicks never exceed impressions (0 violations). Packages were created between 2013-01-24 14:57:06 and 2015-04-30 02:03:39.370000 (timezone unknown, per the paper). Total impressions: 376,529,158; clicks: 5,741,684. The paper does not give per-release impression or click totals, so those are not checked.
+
+### The randomization correction
+
+Tests whose first package was created from 25 June 2013 through the end of 10 January 2014 are dropped, as the authors' correction recommends. That removes **4,907 of 22,743 tests (21.6%)** and 19,845 packages, leaving 17,836 tests. The correction reports 7,004 affected tests, or 22% of the full archive, so the share here is in line. Flagging a test when any of its packages falls in the window gives 4,910; requiring all of them gives 4,906. Shifting both window edges to allow for the unknown timezone gives: -24h: 4,902, -12h: 4,908, +12h: 4,903, +24h: 4,879.
+
+A sample-ratio check backs the correction up. Within each test, a chi-square test of equal impressions across arms gives p < 0.001 in 70.1% of multi-arm tests inside the window and in 0.5% outside it (median p 1.3e-06 vs 0.44).
+
+**A real A/A check.** Some tests contain two arms that showed viewers exactly the same headline, image ID and excerpt. In the kept tests there are 2011 such pairs. If those arms were fairly randomized and clicks were independent, about 5% of them would differ at p < 0.05. 12.9% do (binomial test against 5%: p = 1.3e-42), and the mean squared z-statistic is 1.92 where 1 is expected.
+
+So click counts vary more between identical arms than binomial sampling allows. The data cannot say why (possible reasons: something about the arms not recorded in the archive, or traffic that was not served evenly over time). It means the naive z-tests below, and the simulations that assume binomial noise, are if anything too optimistic. Section 3 includes a sensitivity check that inflates standard errors by this factor.

+# Hypotheses and analysis plan
+
+Written 2026-10-22 at 17:47 EDT, before the full run. Nothing below is edited after the full run
+starts; corrections go in a dated addendum at the end. The commit that adds this file precedes every
+full-run call, so the git history shows the order.
+
+What had been seen when this was written: a pilot on the pilot items only (8 GSM8K planted-error pairs,
+8 TruthfulQA pairs, 6 self-preference problems, 4 MT-bench pairs), excluded from every reported number.
+`qwen3:8b` and `llama3.1:8b` ran every stage; `gemma3:12b` ran generation, base, A/A and
+self-preference on all pilot items and the other stages on 4 items per set; `qwen3:30b-a3b` ran base and
+A/A on 3 items per set and the other stages on 4. The pilot was used to check templates, parsers, timing
+and the grid size. On far too few items to estimate anything, it showed:
+
+- every pairwise verdict of the three main judges parsed, all by the requested `Verdict:` rule; one
+  single-answer output of 112 for `llama3.1:8b` gave no score; `qwen3:30b-a3b` used up its 4,096-token
+  budget thinking about one MT-bench pair (both orders) and gave no verdict (it does not judge MT-bench in
+  the full grid); no other output hit a length cap;
+- a strong pull toward slot A: the same slot in both orders on 44% (`qwen3:8b`), 69% (`llama3.1:8b`) and
+  19% (`gemma3:12b`) of 16 items, almost always slot A; `llama3.1:8b` picked slot A in both orders on
+  all 8 GSM8K pairs;
+- base accuracy (both sets, both orders) of 72%, 66% and 84% for the three main judges, and 6 of 6 for
+  the thinking model;
+- the A/A repeat changed 1 verdict in 96 for the three main judges, but the judge's text differed in 21
+  of 96 repeats: temperature 0 with a fixed seed is not bit-for-bit repeatable on this server;
+- the confident framing was penalised rather than rewarded: with it on the wrong answer, accuracy rose
+  for both 8B judges, and with it on the right answer it fell;
+- verbose padding of the wrong answer cost `llama3.1:8b` 22 pp; markdown changed little;
+- on GSM8K, the planted-error solution scored alone got a mean of 8.1 of 10 from both 8B judges;
+- self-preference on 18 both-right pairs was mixed in sign.
+
+Predictions informed by the pilot are marked (P).
+
+## Primary question
+
+When an LLM judges which of two answers is better and the better one is known, how often does the
+verdict follow something that should not matter (the answer's position, length, confident tone,
+markdown formatting, or the judge's own authorship) rather than correctness, and how much accuracy does
+each cost, measured against the noise of sending the identical prompt twice?
+
+## Definitions
+
+- *Accuracy*: share of (item, order) calls whose verdict picks the right answer; an unparsed verdict
+  counts as wrong.
+- *Consistent*: same answer picked in both orders. *Slot A both* / *slot B both*: the verdict follows the
+  slot rather than the content.
+- *Flip rate* of a condition: share of (item, order) calls whose pick differs from the base call in the
+  same order (an unparsed verdict is its own value). *Floor*: the A/A repeat's flip rate.
+- *Excess*: flip rate minus the floor on the same items, paired by item.
+- *Pull* of a style: how much more often an answer is picked when it carries the style than when plain.
+  On the wrong answer: base accuracy minus accuracy; on the right answer: accuracy minus base accuracy;
+  *mean pull*: the average of the two, paired by item.
+- *Self-preference* of judge X: on pairs of solutions by X and Y, how often X picks its own solution
+  minus how often the third main model Z (neutral) picks X's solution, both orders.
+- *Pointwise accuracy*: share of items where the right answer, scored alone from 1 to 10, scores above
+  the wrong one (a tie counts half).
+- "Main judges" = `qwen3:8b`, `llama3.1:8b`, `gemma3:12b`. "Pooled" = GSM8K and TruthfulQA together,
+  resampled within set.
+
+## Predictions
+
+1. (P) Position bias is common and favours the first slot: on the base prompt, pooled, at least two of
+   the three main judges give the same slot in both orders on at least 20% of items, and for at least
+   two of them `slot A both` exceeds `slot B both` with the interval of the paired difference above
+   zero.
+2. (P) Position bias is larger on GSM8K than on TruthfulQA (lower consistency) for at least two of the
+   three main judges.
+3. The A/A flip rate is under 5% for every judge, pooled.
+4. (P) Verbose padding of the wrong answer lowers accuracy, pooled, with the interval below zero, for at
+   least two of the three main judges.
+5. (P) Confident framing backfires: applied to the wrong answer it does not lower accuracy for any main
+   judge (point estimate at or above zero, pooled), and its mean pull is negative, with the interval
+   below zero, for at least two of the three main judges.
+6. Markdown formatting has the smallest (or tied smallest) absolute mean pull of the three styles for at
+   least two of the three main judges, pooled.
+7. Restyling moves verdicts beyond the noise floor: of the 18 cells (3 main judges x 6 style
+   conditions, pooled), the excess over the A/A repeat has an interval above zero in more than half.
+8. Self-preference: on both-right pairs, the mean of the three main judges' self-preference is above
+   zero, and at least one judge's interval is above zero.
+9. Single-answer scoring misses planted errors: on GSM8K, the planted-error solution scored alone gets a
+   mean of at least 6 of 10 from every main judge, and pairwise accuracy exceeds pointwise accuracy
+   (interval of the paired difference above zero) for at least two of the three main judges. No
+   direction is predicted for TruthfulQA.
+10. Agreement with the MT-bench human majority is between 55% and 80% for every main judge.

+# Hypotheses and analysis plan
+
+Written 2026-10-19 at 11:50 EDT, before the full run. Nothing below is edited after the full run starts;
+corrections go in a dated addendum at the end.
+
+What had been seen when this was written: a pilot on users 0 and 1 (all eight conditions, `qwen3:8b`
+answering), used to check the memory stores, prompts and judge on real transcripts. Those two users are
+excluded from every reported number; the full run uses users 2 to 11. The pilot showed, on 12 questions per
+cell: the plain append store stale on roughly 40% of baseline questions, the overwrite store and the
+rolling summary rarely stale, and the full-context baseline stale on most implied updates. The predictions
+below were written with that in view, so the pilot-informed ones are marked (P).
+
+## Primary question
+
+When a fact about the user changes, how often does an agent with long-term memory answer with the old
+value, and how does that depend on how often the old value was stated, how long ago the update was, how
+the update was phrased, and the memory design?
+
+## Predictions
+
+Stale rate = share of questions answered with an old value. pp = percentage points.
+
+1. Baseline (P). The append-only vector store (a) is stale on 25% or more of baseline questions for every
+   model. Full context (f) is stale on 15% or fewer.
+2. Repetition is the main driver for append stores. For a, stale rate rises from 1 to 10 statements by at
+   least 20 pp for every model. The overwrite store (c) shows little or no repetition effect (under 10 pp),
+   because restatements replace each other. Full context (f) shows a smaller effect than a.
+3. Recency matters little for similarity-only retrieval. For a, gap20 minus gap0 is within the A/A gap,
+   because cosine similarity does not see time and the filler sessions rarely outrank fact entries. For
+   recency-weighted retrieval (d), stale rate rises with the gap (the recency bonus of the update fades).
+4. Implied updates (P) are worse than explicit ones for every system that relies on the model noticing a
+   change: a, b, d, e and f each at least 15 pp more stale. The overwrite store (c) is affected less, because
+   its writer compares the new entry with the old one directly.
+5. A second update (A to B to C) raises the stale rate for the append stores (two old values compete with
+   one current value).
+6. Fixes, against a on baseline questions:
+   - timestamps (b) cut the stale rate by at least 10 pp for the larger models; smaller models use dates
+     less reliably;
+   - overwrite on update (c) cuts it the most among the vector stores, at the price of more "neither"
+     answers when the writer deletes the wrong entry;
+   - recency weighting (d) helps less than timestamps or overwrite;
+   - the rolling summary (e) has a low stale rate but more "hedged" answers that merge old and new values;
+   - write-side cost: c and e need extra writer calls per session; read-side cost: f has by far the longest
+     prompts and b adds tokens for dates.
+7. Retrieval depth: larger k for a puts both values in context more often and raises the hedged rate.
+8. Model size: given the same memories, `qwen3:30b-a3b` is stale less often than the 8B models,
+   mostly when both values are in context.
+9. Answers rarely mention that the fact changed (under 30% of correct answers) except with timestamps or
+   full context.
+
+What would contradict "repetition beats recency in agent memory": a repetition effect for a within the
+A/A gap, or stale rates for a that fall with more statements.
+
+## Analysis plan (fixed in advance)
+
+- Unit of resampling: user (one history family, six probed facts). 95% percentile bootstrap, 2,000 draws.
+  Effects are paired by user and fact.
+- Primary metric: stale rate. Secondary: correct, hedged, neither, mentions-change, and retrieval
+  diagnostics (whether the retrieved entries held the current value, an old value, or both).
+- Primary contrasts: rep10 minus rep1 and gap20 minus gap0 for each system and model; each of b, c, d, e
+  and f minus a on baseline questions. Everything else is secondary and reported without a claim.
+- Noise floors: rewording A/A (`aa` minus `base`, same users and values, different phrasing seed and
+  filler draw) and rerun A/A (`qwen3:8b` baseline questions asked again with the cache bypassed). An effect is
+  reported as real only if its interval excludes zero and its size exceeds the rewording gap for the same
+  model and system.
+- Multiple comparisons: about 7 systems x 4 models x 7 contrasts. No correction; the primary contrasts
+  above are the ones read as confirmatory, the rest as exploratory.
+- Exclusions: none planned. A failed call is retried; if it still fails the run stops rather than dropping
+  the question.
+- Judge audit: blind hand labels on a random sample of 50 answers plus 25 answers that mention both values;
+  agreement is published.
+
+## Run settings
+
+- Writer for every store: `qwen3:8b`. Answering models: `qwen3:8b`, `llama3.1:8b`, `gemma3:12b`,
+  `qwen3:30b-a3b`, as many as time allows, in that order.
+- Temperature 0, seed 7, `num_ctx` 8192, `think: false` for qwen3, `num_predict` caps per call type.
+- Embeddings `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`; k = 5 (3 and 10 for a on baseline); recency decay 0.95 per session
+  with equal weights; overwrite shows the writer the top 3 similar entries per new fact, at most 8.
+- Users 2 to 11 (10 users x 6 facts = 60 questions per cell).
+

+# Hypotheses and analysis plan
+
+Written 2026-10-20 at 16:33 EDT, before the full run. Nothing below is edited after the full run starts;
+corrections go in a dated addendum at the end.
+
+What had been seen when this was written: a pilot on 6 pilot items (2 per task) with `qwen3:8b`,
+`llama3.1:8b` and `gemma3:12b`, every variant, used to check the templates and the parsers on real
+outputs, plus 10 answer-only GSM8K prompts on two models (which showed that answer-only maths is near
+chance for these models, so worked reasoning stays in). The pilot items (10 per task) are excluded from
+every reported number. The pilot showed, on far too few items to estimate anything: `llama3.1:8b`
+changing its multiple-choice answer under several rephrasings of one question, the other two models
+stable on the same items, and every output parseable. Predictions informed by that are marked (P).
+
+## Primary question
+
+When a task prompt is rephrased in ways that should not change its meaning, how often does the parsed
+answer change, how often does it change from right to wrong, which kinds of rephrasing matter most, and
+is the best-scoring prompt variant a real improvement or a lucky draw?
+
+## Predictions
+
+Flip rate = share of items whose parsed answer differs from the answer under the base prompt. pp =
+percentage points. "Floor" = the flip rate when the base prompt is sent a second time.
+
+1. Averaged over all rephrasings, every model's flip rate is at least 5%, with an interval above its
+   A/A rate.
+2. The A/A flip rate (same prompt, temperature 0, fixed seed) is under 2% for every model.
+3. Option order is among the three kinds of rephrasing with the highest flip rate for most models
+   (prior work on option-order sensitivity).
+4. Politeness and a single typo in the instruction are not distinguishable from the A/A repeat for
+   most models.
+5. Flips are mostly sideways: the net accuracy change of rephrasing (wrong to right minus right to
+   wrong) is within 3 pp of zero for every model. The base prompt is not specially tuned.
+6. GSM8K, where the answer comes after a long worked solution, has the highest flip rate of the three
+   tasks.
+7. Winner's curse for prompts: picking the best of the 11 (13 for MMLU) variants on half the items and
+   scoring it on the other half, the held-out gain over the base prompt is less than half the gain seen
+   on the selection half, averaged over model-task cells, and the middle 95% of held-out gains across
+   random splits covers zero in most cells.
+8. `qwen3:30b-a3b` (run with thinking on) flips less than `qwen3:8b` on the same items and variants.
+   This is confounded with thinking.
+9. (P) `llama3.1:8b` has the highest average flip rate of the models with the full grid.
+
+What would contradict "harmless rephrasings change answers often": average flip rates within the A/A
+floor, or flips confined to option shuffles.
+
+## Analysis plan (fixed in advance)
+
+- Unit of resampling: item. All rephrasings of an item, and its A/A repeat, are paired with the same
+  item's base prompt. 95% percentile bootstrap, 2,000 draws; pooled over tasks, items are resampled
+  within each task.
+- Primary metrics: flip rate, right-to-wrong and wrong-to-right rates (shares of all items), accuracy.
+  Secondary: per-item accuracy spread (always right, always wrong, mixed), conditional rates, parse-rule
+  shares, length-cap hits.
+- Floor rule: a kind of rephrasing is said to change answers only if its flip rate minus the A/A flip rate
+  on the same items has an interval above zero.
+- Kinds: synonyms (2 variants), instruction order (2), formatting (bullets, answer marker), politeness (1),
+  typo (1), system placement (1), output-format wording (1), option order (2, multiple choice only).
+  An item's value for a kind with two variants is the mean over both.
+- Best prompt: per model and task, 2,000 random half splits; the best variant on the selection half

+- Meaning preservation: hand-written templates, automated checks that each rendered prompt contains the

+- Multiple comparisons: about 8 kinds x 4 models. No correction; predictions 1 to 7 are read as

+# Hypotheses and analysis plan
+
+> **DRAFT.** Written 2026-10-23, before any model call: no pilot has run, and the predictions below come

+
+What had been seen when this draft was written: nothing from any model. The harness was tested end to end
+against a stub that returns canned tool-call responses (tests in `tests/`). The predictions draw on the
+templates (read from the local model blobs, without calling the server): the llama3.1:8b template writes the
+tool list only into the last user message and tells the model to answer with a function call whenever tools
+are present; the gemma3:12b template has no tool support, so it runs under a prompted JSON protocol.
+
+## Primary question
+
+Given a handful of tools and a request, how often does a local model call the right tool with the right
+arguments, only when a tool is needed, carry values through two- and three-step chains, and recover from a
+tool error? How much does each of five interface factors change that: the number of tools offered,
+description quality, tool names, argument schema strictness and error message style?
+
+## Definitions
+
+- *Success*: the final answer contains every required fact, the state is exactly as required (no change
+  that was not asked for), every required call was made with the reference arguments (after the
+  normalisation the tool applies), and a `none` task called no tool. Definitions of every other measure and
+  of the outcome labels are in `src/toolrel/check.py` and the README.
+- *Arm*: a model under one protocol (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, gemma3:12b (prompted), qwen3:30b-a3b
+  (thinking); and qwen3:8b (prompted), the bridge). *Main arms*: the first three.
+- *Effect* of a condition: its success minus baseline success, paired by task.
+- *Floor rule*: an effect counts when its 95% interval excludes zero and its size exceeds the arm's A/A flip
+  rate (the share of baseline episodes whose success differs when the identical episode is run again).
+- *Recovery*: success among episodes in which at least one tool error came back. *Fixable* errors: bad id
+  format, misspelt name, clashing booking, timeout. *Cannot be done*: cancelling a shipped order, a forecast
+  beyond the forecast window.
+
+## Predictions
+
+Draft thresholds; (T) marks those that come from the chat templates rather than from intuition.
+
+1. At baseline, single-call tasks succeed on at least 85% of tasks for every native main model (qwen3:8b,
+   llama3.1:8b).
+2. At baseline, three-step chains succeed less often than single calls (chain3 minus single, interval below
+   zero, categories resampled separately) for every main model.
+3. (T) At baseline, llama3.1:8b calls a tool on at least 25% of `none` tasks, and more often than qwen3:8b
+   (paired by task, interval above zero).
+4. On error tasks, bare error codes lower success compared with errors that say how to recover (interval
+   below zero, beyond the floor) for at least two main models.
+5. Twenty tools instead of eight lower success (interval below zero, beyond the floor) for at least two main
+   models.
+6. Three tools instead of eight make no difference that counts under the floor rule for any main model.
+7. Vague tool names lower success (interval below zero, beyond the floor) for at least two main models, and
+   by more than terse descriptions do (point estimates) for at least two.
+8. With free-string arguments, the share of tasks whose required calls all had the right arguments falls
+   (interval below zero, beyond the floor) for at least two main models.
+9. At baseline, at most 2% of episodes call a tool that was not offered, for every main model.
+10. With errors that say how to recover, at least 70% of error-task episodes in which a fixable error came
+    back end in success, for every main model.
+11. At baseline, at least 80% of the tasks that cannot be done end with the model telling the user so and
+    changing nothing, for every main model.
+12. The A/A flip rate is under 3% for every arm.

+  single-call tasks. Two-step chains: `qwen3:8b` 25%, `llama3.1:8b` 0%, `gemma3:12b` 35%. Three-step
